                             O R D E R
1. The  petitioners  are  in  custody  in
connection with FIR No. 54 of 2011 dated
22nd November, 2011 registered at Police
Station Special Cell, New Delhi for the
offences  punishable  under  Sections  471,
489B, 489C, and 120B of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860; Section 25 of the Arms Act,
1959; Sections 17, 18, 18A, 18B, 19 and 20
of  the  Unlawful  Activities  (Prevention)
Act,  1967;  Sections  3,  4,  and  5  of
Explosive  Substances  Act,  1908;  and
Section 12 of the Passports Act, 1967.
2. The respective applications for bail
preferred by the petitioners under Section
SLP(Crl)No(s).  11369/2026
2

--- Page 108 ---
43D(5)  of  the  Unlawful  Activities
(Prevention) Act, 1967 came to be rejected
by the learned trial Court. The appeals
preferred thereagainst under Section 21 of
the  National  Investigation  Agency  Act,
2008, questioning the orders passed by the
learned trial Court were dismissed by the
High Court of Delhi by a common judgment
and order dated 24th April, 2026. Aggrieved
thereby, the petitioners have approached
this Court by way of the present Special
Leave Petitions.
3. We  have  heard  and  considered  the
submissions  advanced  by  learned  counsel
for the petitioners, and Mr. Anil Kaushik,
learned  Additional  Solicitor  General
appearing for the State (NCT of Delhi) and
have perused the record.
4. The Special Cell, during the course of
investigation in the said FIR, arrested a
Pakistani national, Mohd. Qateel Siddiqui,
on  the  intervening  night  of  21 st/22nd
November,  2011.  During  the  course  of
SLP(Crl)No(s).  11369/2026
3

--- Page 109 ---
investigation,  the  said  Mohd.  Qateel
Siddiqui  allegedly  made  disclosures
regarding the establishment of a Rajasthan
Module of the Indian Mujahideen to carry
out  terrorist  activities  in  and  around
Delhi  and  further  disclosed  that  its
members were in possession of consignments
of explosives.
5. Pursuant to the said information, the
premises  of  the  petitioner-Mohd.  Saquib
Ansari at Jodhpur were searched on 23 rd
March,  2014,  during  which  gunpowder,
ammonium  nitrate,  detonators  and  other
articles  allegedly  used  for  the
preparation  of  explosive  devices  were
recovered and seized. These articles were
handed  over  to  the  Rajasthan  ATS,
consequent to which, a separate case being
FIR No. 113/2014 came to be registered at
PS Pratap Nagar, Jodhpur, for the offences
punishable under Sections 4, 5 and 6 of
the  Explosive  Substances  Act,  1908;
Sections 16, 17, 18, 18A, 18B, 19, 20, 23
SLP(Crl)No(s).  11369/2026
4

and  38  of  the  Unlawful  Activities
(Prevention) Act, 1967; and Sections 120B,
121, 121A, 122, 212, 465, 468 and 471 of

6. Likewise,  explosives  and  IED-making
materials  were  recovered  from  the
possession  of  co-accused  Waqar  Azhar
[petitioner  in  SLP  (Crl.)  No.11414  of
2026] at Jaipur.
7. The  recovered  articles  were  handed
over to the Rajasthan ATS/SOG, leading to
the registration of FIR No. 03/2014 at

for the offences punishable under Sections
4 and 5 of the Explosive Substances Act,

1967 read with Section 120B of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860.

remained in custody ever since.  They have

been granted bail in connection with the

petitioners  in  the  present  case,  has
already been enlarged on bail.
15. Having  appreciated  the  submissions
advanced at bar, and upon going through
the record, we find that the petitioners
have, more or less, been implicated in
three  separate  FIRs  for  overlapping
allegations.
16. In  FIR  No.  03/2014  registered  at
Police Station CID/SOG, Jaipur, both the
petitioners  were  convicted,  and  their
sentences have since been suspended by the
High Court. Both the petitioners have also
been granted bail in connection with FIR
No.113/2014 registered at PS Pratap Nagar,
Jodhpur.  Consequently,  the  continued
incarceration of the petitioners is solely
on account of FIR No. 54/2011 registered
SLP(Crl)No(s).  11369/2026
8

--- Page 114 ---
at PS Special Cell, New Delhi.  We have
checked the status of the trial from the
proceedings  available  on  the  e-Courts
Services Portal. An application for bail
preferred by co-accused Mohd. Kafeel came
to be rejected by the learned trial Court
vide order dated 20 th July, 2026, wherein
it has been noticed that the examination
of PW-68 was continuing out of the 197
prosecution  witnesses  proposed  to  be
examined. The proceedings further reveal
that from January, 2025 till date, only
two witnesses have been examined, one of
whom has been examined only in part. The
progress of the trial has been extremely
slow, and there appears to be no prospect
of the trial being concluded in the near
future.
17. As per the counter-affidavit of the
respondents, as many as 25 accused have
been arrested in the present case. Having
regard  to  the  overall  facts  and
circumstances,  particularly the fact that
SLP(Crl)No(s).  11369/2026
9

--- Page 115 ---
the co-accused Mohd. Maroof has already
been enlarged on bail ; that the sentences
of  both  the  petitioners  have  been
suspended in the case arising from FIR No.
03/2014 registered at PS CID/SOG, Jaipur
wherein they were convicted by the special
Court at Rajasthan; that the petitioners
have been granted bail in connection with
the  FIR  No.113/2014  registered  at  PS
Pratap Nagar, Jodhpur; coupled with the
slow progress of trial, we feel that the
continued incarceration of the petitioners
in this case is grossly violative of the
right to liberty enshrined under Article
21 of the Constitution of India.
18. Accordingly,  we  direct  that  the
petitioners be released on bail, on such
terms and conditions as may be imposed by
the trial Court, in connection with FIR
No.54 of 2011 dated 22 nd November, 2011
registered at PS Special Cell, New Delhi,
subject to their not being required in any
other case.

Mr. Himinder Lal, AOR (IMPL)
     UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Kerala  Public  Service  Commission  issued  a
notification dated 16.08.2023 for recruitment to the
posts  of  Associate  Professor  and  Professor  in
Government  Homoeopathic  Medical  Colleges.  Essential
qualifications  for  eligibility,  which  were  in
conformity with extant Service Rules of the State of
Kerala, were specified as under:
(i) Postgraduate Degree in Homoeopathy
recognized by the Central Council of
Homoeopathy and included in the Second
Schedule of the Homoeopathy Central
Act, 1973; 
(ii) 4 years teaching experience in
the concerned subject in any of the
recognized  Homoeopathy  Medical
Colleges  in  Kerala  or  recognized
Government  Homoeopathic  Medical
3

--- Page 120 ---
Colleges in any other States; and
(iii)  Permanent  registration  with
Travancore Cochin Medical Council.
2. A bunch of candidates filed petition(s) before
the Tribunal challenging the qualification specified in
the advertisement in respect of the qualifying teaching
experience to the extent it limited the field of
teaching  experience  to  any  of  the  recognized
Homoeopathic Medical Colleges in Kerala or recognized
Government Homoeopathic Medical Colleges in any other
States. Their case was that under Section 33 of the
Homoeopathy Central Council Act, 1973, “Homoeopathy”
Central  Council  (minimum  standard  requirement  of
Homoeopathic  Colleges  and  attached  Hospitals)
Regulations, 2013 (for short, 2013 Regulations) were
framed wherein the qualifying teaching experience was
not limited to a college located within the State of
Kerala or to a State/ Government college of any other
State as is specified in the advertisement.  It was
their case that the State Service Rules were to apply
only if they were not in conflict with the Central
Council Regulations i.e., 2013 Regulations.  
3. During pendency of the proceedings before the
Tribunal an ‘erratum’ notification dated 16.11.2023 was
4

--- Page 121 ---
issued which altered the qualifications specified in
the advertisement to read as under:
“Post  Graduate  qualification  in
Homoeopathy  with  four  years  of
teaching  experience  as  Assistant
Professor/Lecturer  in  the  concerned
subject in a Homoeopathic College of
Degree Level.  The qualification shall
be  the one  included in  the Second
Schedule  of  Homoeopathy  Central
Council Act, 1973.”  
4. Pursuant  to  the  erratum  notification,  the
grievance of all those who had petitioned to the
Tribunal  against  the  advertised  qualifications  was
resolved and, therefore, those petitions were disposed
of.
5. Aggrieved by the amended qualifications specified
in the erratum notification, writ petition(s), lead
petition being O.P. (KAT) No.470/2024, were filed by
another set of candidates before the High Court of
Kerala.
6. The High Court took the view that Central Council
Regulations i.e., 2013 Regulations only set out the
minimum  eligibility  qualifications  to  ensure  that
5

--- Page 122 ---
minimum  standard  requirements  qua infrastructure,
teaching and training facilities referred to in the
Regulations 4 to 13 are maintained. Moreover, 2013
Regulations do not proscribe State supplementing those
minimum  qualifications  by  laying  higher  or  more
specific qualifications. Therefore, the extant State
Service Rules only supplement the 2013 Regulations and
in no way dilute the minimum standards set out therein.
Consequently, it set aside the erratum notification
which was at variance with the extant State Service
Rules. T he  High  Court  further  directed  the  Public
Service  Commission  to  proceed  and  conclude  the
recruitment  exercise  in  terms  of  the  original
notification dated 16.08.2023. 
7. Aggrieved by the order of the High Court, these
petitions have been filed.
8. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and
have perused the materials available on record.
9. The learned counsel for the petitioners contended
that both State Service Rules and Central Council
Regulations (i.e., 2013 Regulations) are under the Acts
which have been enacted by the Parliament and State
Legislature, respectively, under Entry 25 of List III
6

--- Page 123 ---
(i.e., the Concurrent List). Since both operate on the
same field, the Central Regulations, in the event of
conflict with the State Rules, will prevail.  The
erratum notification thus ensures that there is no
conflict between the two and it in no way dilutes the
minimum  standards,  rather  increases  the  zone  of
consideration to ensure that there is a larger pool of
candidates  available  for  selection.  In  such
circumstances,  the  High  Court  ought  not  to  have
interfered with the erratum notification.
10. Per contra, on behalf of the respondents who were
the writ petitioners before the High Court, it is
submitted that the Central Council Regulations do not
prescribe the qualifications, they set out the minimum
qualifications necessary for the teaching faculty. In
such  circumstances,  the  State  had  the  power  to
prescribe  the  qualifications;  and  since  those
prescribed qualifications are in no way less than the
minimum qualifications set out in the Central Council
Regulations, those prescribed qualifications, as it
existed in the extant State Service Rules, cannot be
diluted by a notification.  
11. We have considered the rival submissions and have
gone through the Central Council Regulations, 2013 as
7

--- Page 124 ---
well as the extant Service Rules, 2019. A plain reading
of Regulation 3 of the 2013 Regulations would indicate
that they set out the minimum standard requirements of
infrastructure and teaching and training facilities
which  find  reference  in  Regulations  4  to  13.
Consequently,  Regulation  12,  which  sets  out  the
qualifications of the teaching faculty, would have to
be read in conjunction with Regulation 3 to understand
whether it prescribes the qualifications for the post
or the minimum eligibility for the post to maintain the
requisite standard. 
12. When we read Regulation 12 in conjunction with
Regulation 3, it becomes clear that the object of the
Central Council Regulations is to set out the minimum
eligibility qualifications. They do not proscribe the
State  to  supplement  those  minimum  eligibility
qualifications  by  prescribing  qualification
requirements over and above the minimum set out in the
Central Council Regulations.
13. The 2019 Service Rules do not dilute the minimum
qualifications specified in the 2013 Regulations. In
our view, therefore, the High court was correct in its
view that they supplement the minimum qualifications.
14. As it not in issue that the original notification
8

--- Page 125 ---
dated 16.08.2023 specified the essential qualifications
as specified in the extant Service Rules, 2019, and the
erratum notification is at variance with the 2019
Service Rules, the view taken by the High Court cannot
be faulted.
15. The special leave petitions are, accordingly,
dismissed.
16. All pending applications including application(s)
for impleadment shall stand disposed of.
  (KAVITA PAHUJA)                          (SAPNA BANSAL)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                   COURT MASTER (NSH)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
       CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION

NEHA SHARMA                                    Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
ANKUR SHARMA                                   Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. The petitioner has filed the petition under Section 25 of
the Code of Civil Procedure Code before this Court seeking
transfer of the case, details of which are as under:
“Matrimonial Suit No. 731/2024 titled as “Ankur
Sharma Vs. Neha Sharma” pending in Family Court-
02 at Ajmer to the Family Court at Saket, New
Delhi.”    
2. During the pendency of aforesaid transfer petition, the
parties were referred to the Supreme Court Mediation Centre vide
order dated 04.02.2026.  By virtue of the mediation, the parties
have arrived at a settlement and they have decided to part ways
on certain terms and conditions which are delineated in the
settlement agreement dated 25.03.2026, which has been signed by
both the parties, their respective counsel and the Mediator,
copy of which has been filed by the Supreme Court Mediation
Centre.
3. Learned  counsel  for  the  parties  has  filed  a  joint
application being IA No. 117568/2026 with the following prayers:
“a)  Invoke the powers under Article 142 of the
Constitution of India and dissolve the marriage
between  the  Petitioner-Wife  and  the  Respondent-

--- Page 136 ---
2
Husband by a decree of divorce by mutual consent, in
terms of the Settlement Agreement dated 25.03.2026;
b) Quash and/or direct closure of all pending cases,
FIRs complaints, proceedings or litigations of any
nature whatsoever whether civil or criminal, filed
by the Petitioner-Wife and/or her family members
against the Respondent-Husband and/or his family
members, and vice versa, arising out of or in
connection with the present matrimonial dispute;
c)  Grant  permanent  custody  of  both  the  minor
children to the Respondent-Husband, in terms of the
Settlement Agreement, the same having been agreed to
by both the parties in the best interest and welfare
of the children; 
4. Further,  the  terms  and  conditions  and  the  relevant
paragraphs as set out in Settlement Agreement dated 25.03.2026
are as under: 
“SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT
“This Settlement Agreement is entered into between
Petitioner- Ms. Neha Sharma W/o Mr Ankur Sharma D/o
Sh. Suresh Sharma R/o 14a, Astha Apartment, 3rd floor,
Arjun Nagar, Safdarjung Enclave, New Delhi 110029
(hereinafter referred to as Petitioner-Wife) and Mr.
Ankur Sharma S/o Sri Nathu Lal Sharma R/o B-72,
Chhatri  Yojna,  Vaishali  Nagar,  Ajmer-305001
(hereinafter referred to as Respondent-Husband).
Whereas  the  marriage  between  the  petitioner  and
respondent husband was solemnized as per Hindu rites
and ceremonies on 01.11.2009 at Delhi.
2. Whereas, from the wedlock of the parties have two
children, daughter Ms Mishka Sharma (Date of birth
24.03.2013) and son Master Aahan Sharma (Date of birth
11.12.2016). Both the children are residing with their
father i.e. Respondent-Husband

--- Page 137 ---
3
3. Whereas, owing to the matrimonial dispute, the
parties have been living separately since 17.12.2021.
4. Whereas a divorce petition HMA No. 1321 of 2025
titled as " Neha Sharma Vs Ankur Sharma" under Section
13(1)(ia) of Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 for dissolution
of marriage was filed by the Petitioner-wife before
the Ld. Principal Judge, Family Court, South, Saket
District Court, New Delhi.
5. Whereas, apart from the above Petitioner-wife has
filed following legal cases which are still under
consideration of the respective court:
i. CT case 1274/2022 titled Neha Sharma v. Ankur

II. CR Case 5970/2025 titled State v. Ankur Sharma Uls
498A,509,406,34,506 IPC pending before the Ld. Court

Court Delhi.
6. Whereas, Respondent- husband has filed following
legal cases which are still under consideration of the
respective court:
1. RCR case No. 731/2024 pending before the Ld. Family
court number 2, Ajmer.
ii. Maintenance case No. 45/2026 pending before the
Ld. Family court number 2, Ajmer
7. Whereas, the present transfer petition has been
filed for transfer of RCR case No. 731/2024 from Ld.
Family court number 2, Ajmer to Delhi.
8. Whereas the Hon'ble Supreme Court vide Order dated
04.02.2026 in Transfer Petition (Civil) No. 2455 of
2025 has referred the matter to the Supreme Court

Centre appointed undersigned as mediator.
9. Whereas comprehensive mediation sessions were held
between the parties and their respective advocates on
12.02.2026, 16.02.2026, 25.02.2026 in both physical
and virtual mode. Both the parties has reached the
settlement between them today i.e.25.03.2026 where
both parties are present physically for signing of the
present Settlement Agreement.

--- Page 138 ---
4
10.  Both  the  parties  hereto  have  arrived  at  an
amicable  settlement  on  the  following  terms  and
conditions  for  dissolution  of  marriage  by  mutual
consent:
A) That the respondent husband has agreed to pay Rs.
5,00,000/- (Rupees five Lakh only) to petitioner-wife
towards full and final settlement of all the claims
regarding  dowry,  stridhan,  permanent  alimony  and
maintenance (past, present and future) and any other
claim whatsoever.
B) That, respondent-husband has also agreed to hand
over motor car with registration no. DL10CK 6230, in
good condition, to the petitioner-wife.
C) That the custody of both the children shall remain
with their father, the respondent-husband who shall
bear all education, higher education, marriage and
other  miscellaneous  expenses  of  the  children.
Petitioner-wife has agreed that she does not wish to
have  any  visitation  rights  with  the  children  or
interaction with the children in future and shall not
interfere in their life in any manner.
D) That the Petitioner-wife has agreed to pay Rs.
10,00,000/-(Rupees  ten  Lakh  only)  to  respondent-
husband as her contribution towards expenses that he
will incur or education, higher education, marriage
and other miscellaneous expenses of their children.
E) That, the parties will, within next fortnight move
a joint application before the Hon'ble Supreme Court
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India for
invoking inherent powers of the Hon'ble Supreme Court
praying for divorce by mutual consent as parties are
staying separately since 17.12.2021 i.e. for more than
four years and there is an irretrievable breakdown of
the marriage. In the said application the party will
also pray for the quashing/closure of all pending
cases or proceedings of any nature whatsoever, whether
civil or criminal, FIRs, complaints, filed or caused
to be filed by the Respondent Husband and/or any
member of his family against the Petitioner Wife
and/or any member of her family, and vice versa,
arising out of or in connection with the present
marriage and matrimonial disputes, whether already
disclosed or previously not disclosed.
F) That after the grant of divorce, they will not
interfere in each other's social life or personal life
by any means or mode through social media, online or
offline and will also ensure that members of either

--- Page 139 ---
5
family not get indulge with any such activity.
G) That during their conjugal relationship, both the
parties have taken photographs or videos together or
of each other which may be in their mobile phones or
laptops or in social media accounts which might not
have been deleted yet. Both the parties have agreed
that they shall delete all the photographs and videos
of each other either single or joint and shall not use
these photographs or share them public places or in
derogatory manner against the consent and approval of
the  other  party  and  shall  destroy  the  same,  if
required.
H) That the parties further undertake not misuse any
personal identification details of the other party,
such as Aadhaar number, PAN, passport details, bank
account details, passwords or other sensitive personal
data, and shall not share such details with any third
persons. 
I) That nothing contained in this agreement shall
prejudice or affect any legal rights of either party,
nor  shall  it  extend  to  or  cover  any  fresh  and
independent cause of action that may arise after the
date of this Agreement. 
11. That on a conjoint reading of Clauses 9(A), 9(B)
and 9(C), it is agreed that the Petitioner-Wife shall
pay a sum of Rs.5,00,000/-(Rupees Five Lakh only) to
the  Respondent-Husband,  and  the  Respondent-Husband
shall hand over the motor car bearing Registration No.
DL10CK 6230, in good and running condition, to the
Petitioner-Wife. Both parties have mutually agreed to
the  said  arrangement.  The  Respondent-Husband  has

their daughter, Ms. Mishka Sharma, and has undertaken
to create a Fixed Deposit Receipt (FDR) of the said

for her higher education and/or marriage. Accordingly,
the Petitioner-Wife has handed over Demand Draft No.
508219  dated  23.03.2026  drawn  on  ICICI  Bank  for
Rs.5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakh only) in the name of
their daughter Ms. Mishka Sharma to the Respondent-
Husband.
12. That both the parties have agreed that neither of
them shall initiate any further legal proceedings,
complaint, or action against each other or against the
family members of the other in respect of their
matrimonial dispute in future.
13. That subject to the aforesaid terms, the parties

--- Page 140 ---
6
have amicably resolved all disputes arising out of

14.  That  by  signing  this  Agreement,  the  parties

claims or demands against each other, including but
not  limited  to  claims  relating  to  maintenance,
alimony,  stridhan,  or  any  movable  or  immovable

between them have been amicably settled through the

15. That both the parties undertake to abide by the

Agreement, which has been arrived at out of their own
free will and volition, without any coercion, duress,

16. However, in the event of breach of any provision

initiating appropriate legal proceedings, or seeking
specific performance. In such an event, this Agreement
shall stand null and void and the parties shall revert
to  their  respective  legal  positions  as  If  this

17. That the contents of this Settlement Agreement
have been read over and explained to the parties by

18. That the Respondent-Husband acknowledges receipt
of Demand Draft No. 508219 dated 23.03.2026 drawn on

19. That this Settlement Agreement has been executed

Supreme Court Mediation Centre, New Delhi.”
5. We  have  taken  the  Joint  Application  and  Settlement
Agreement dated 25.03.2026 on record. 
6. Having considered the matter in detail and having perused
the Settlement Agreement & Joint Application, which is also
supported by the affidavits of Ms. Neha Sharma and Mr. Ankur
Sharma, we are of the view that this is a fit case for
exercising power under Article 142 of the Constitution of India
to dissolve the marriage between the parties. Consequently, the
marriage between the parties which was solemnized on 01.11.2009
stands dissolved by a decree of divorce by mutual consent. 
7. We further direct that the following cases pending between
the parties before the courts below stand disposed of in terms
of the consent terms recorded in our order :
“i. CT case 1274/2022 titled Neha Sharma v.
Ankur Sharma & Ors. U/s 12 DV Act pending before
the Ld. Court of Ms. Neetika Kapoor, JMFC,
South, Saket District Court Delhi.
II. CR Case 5970/2025 titled State v. Ankur
Sharma  Uls  498A,509,406,34,506  IPC  pending
before the Ld. Court of Ms. Neetika Kapoor,
JMFC, South, Saket District Court Delhi.
III.  RCR case No. 731/2024 pending before the
Ld. Family court number 2, Ajmer.
IV. Maintenance case No. 45/2026 pending before
the Ld. Family court number 2, Ajmer”
8. Copy of this order shall be sent to the respective Courts
as mentioned in the above Paragraph for follow up action.
9. In  view  of  the  above,  Transfer  Petition  and  Joint
Application being IA No. 117568/2026 are disposed of. The

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
@ SLP (CRL.) NO.3685/2026
LALAN RAY @ LALAN RAI @ LALLAN RAI APPELLANT
                        VERSUS
STATE OF BIHAR             RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant  who  has  been  arraigned  as  an
accused in FIR No.133/2023 registered for the
offences punishable under Section 302 read with
Section  34  of  the  Indian  Penal  Code,  1860
(“IPC”), namely, for allgedly having murdered his
daughter to keep the honour of the family (as per
the prosecution’s case) is seeking for bail.
4. It is the case of the prosecution that minor
daughter of the appellant and his wife (in the
1

--- Page 153 ---
present FIR) had been assaulted by Dhananjay Rai
and others alongwith appellant and Krishna Devi
and as such FIR No.133/2023 came to be registered
for the offences punishable under Sections 302
and 34 of the IPC. It is apt to note at this
juncture that the deceased is said to have been
assaulted earlier also by Dhananjay Rai resulting
in FIR No.675/2022 being registered against the
persons. The further case of the prosecution is
that  on  12.03.2023  around  06:30  p.m.,  the
deceased went to fetch water for daily use of the
family and never returned and the appellant after
returning from the local market searched for his
daughter and after search did not yield any
result, appellant alongwith Ravi Kumar went to
Gadhka P.S. around 09:00 p.m. and after such
reporting  of  the  incident,  investigation  was
taken up and appellant and his wife alongwith
Manoj Rai were arrested. Based on the disclosure
statement of the said Manoj Rai, the appellant
came to be implicated in FIR No.133/2023. In
2

--- Page 154 ---
fact,  the  appellant’s  son  is  said  to  have
approached  National  Human  Rights  Commission
(“NHRC")  seeking  fair  investigation  and
protection  of  the  family  which  has  been
registered and summons having been issued to the
jurisdictional police. It is the case of the
appellant  that  the  appellant  and  his  family
members are under constant threat by the local
police and as such they have left Bihar and are
now staying at Noida. On the basis of the report
filed by the Investigating Officer, NHRC is said
to  have  passed  an  order  on  10.08.2023  for
ensuring fair investigation in FIR No.133/2023
and also FIR No.675/2022 referred to hereinsupra.
5. As noticed hereinabove, based on Manoj Rai’s
statement wherein he alleged that he alongwith
the son and parents of the deceased victim had
killed the deceased on 12.03.2023 on the ground
that she was having an affair with a boy called
Abhijeet Kumar of the same village. The statement
of Akhilesh Rai, nephew of the accused who also
3

--- Page 155 ---
gave  a  statement  under  Section  164  of  the
Criminal  Procedure  Code,  1973  before  the
jurisdictional Magistrate of having seen Manoj
Rai and his son Sonu Rai taking the deceased to
their house in the night and later on, the
victim’s body being found are the cumulative
facts which persuaded the jurisdictional police
to arraign the present appellant as accused.
6. It is an undisputed fact that there was an
earlier  FIR  being  FIR  No.675/2022  which  was
registered by the deceased against Dhananjay Rai
and others on account of assault by them and it
is this FIR which the NHRC seems to have also
directed for investigation being carried out to
reach its logical end. In this factual scenario
as to what was the actual role played by the
appellant in the alleged crime requires to be
examined. The appellant’s wife who has also been
arraigned as an accused as well as Manoj Rai who
is said to be the prime accused having already
been enlarged on bail, the appellant would be
4

--- Page 156 ---
entitled for being released on bail on the ground
of parity. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed and
appellant is ordered to be released on bail on
such terms and conditions as the jurisdictional
Sessions Court may deem fit to impose including
the condition of directing him to appear before
the trial court on all dates of hearing except
when exempted. 
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.10358-10361/2010
T. GOVINDARAJ AND ORS.                  Appellant(s)
VERSUS
R. SUBRATHINAM AND ORS.             Respondent(s)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 5566/2014
O R D E R
1. The delay in filing the application(s) for setting aside
the abatement is condoned and abatement stands set aside.
2. The delay in filing the application(s) for substitution
is  condoned  and  the  application(s)  for  substitution
stand(s) allowed.
3. The appellants in Civil Appeal Nos. 10358-10361/2010,
T. Govindaraj along with his sons P.T. Rajan, Kandaswamy
and T.G. Shanmugasundaram were the Defendants before the
Trial Court. The respondents in Civil Appeal Nos. 10358-
10361/2010, R. Subrathinam and others are the legal
representatives  of  the  original  1st  Plaintiff,  late
Booshanambal.
4. The properties in dispute are ‘A’ Schedule Property which
are Agricultural lands and ‘B’ Schedule Property which is
a Residential house property.  Both 'A' and 'B' schedule
properties were jointly held and enjoyed by Kandaswamy

--- Page 160 ---
2
Pillai and his wife Thirumalai Ammal. On Kandaswamy
Pillai’s death in 1933, the properties devolved upon his
son  Thiruvenkadam  Pillai  and  grandson  T.  Govindaraj
(appellant  herein/Defendant  No.  1  before  the  Trial
Court).
5. Thiruvenkadam  Pillai  had  one  son,  T.  Govindaraj
(appellant  herein/Defendant  No.  1  before  the  Trial
Court),  and  one  daughter,  Booshanambal  (original
plaintiff before the Trial Court). Thiruvenkadam Pillai
passed away on 04.02.1963.
6. The original Plaintiff, Booshanambal, instituted O.S. No.
25 of 2005 seeking partition and 1/2 share in ‘A’ and ‘B’
schedule  properties,  alleging  that  the  properties
belonged absolutely to her grandmother Thirumalai Ammal,
and that her father Thiruvenkadam Pillai died intestate.
7. The Defendants resisted the suit contending that the
properties were ancestral coparcenary properties (wherein
Thiruvenkadam Pillai and Defendant No. 1 held equal 1/2
shares)  and  that  Thiruvenkadam  Pillai  executed  a
registered Will dated 01.02.1963 bequeathing his 1/2
share to his grandsons (Defendant No. 2 & Defendant No.
3). The Defendants also filed a counter-claim to evict
the  Plaintiffs  from  ‘B’  schedule  property  and  for
damages.
8. The Trial Court was pleased to hold that the suit
properties were not the absolute self-acquired properties
of  Thirumalai  Ammal,  but  ancestral/joint  family

--- Page 161 ---
3
coparcenary properties. It also upheld the validity and
execution of the registered Will dated 01.02.1963 (Ex.
B46)  executed  by  Thiruvenkadam  Pillai  in  favour  of
Defendant No. 2 and Defendant No. 3. The Trial Court
further held that Plaintiff No. 1 occupied a portion of
‘B’ schedule property only as a permissive licensee,
which lapsed upon her death. 
9. Hence, the Trial Court dismissed the suit for partition
and held that the Plaintiffs are not entitled to any
share in the suit properties.  It also partially decreed
the Defendants' counter-claim by granting a mandatory
injunction directing the Plaintiffs to vacate and hand
over possession of ‘B’ schedule property within one year,
but did not grant damages.
10. The High Court, vide the impugned order, allowed the
Plaintiffs'  appeal  in  part.  On  the  other  hand,  it
dismissed the Defendants’ counter-claim for eviction and
damages in toto, as well as their Cross-Objection.
11. The High Court, while doing so, was pleased to
affirm the Trial Court's finding that Thirumalai Ammal
was not the absolute owner and that Thiruvenkadam Pillai
and Defendant No. 1 held equal 1/2 shares as coparceners.
The High Court specifically held that the registered Will
dated 01.02.1963 (Ex. B46) was surrounded by suspicious
circumstances as the testator died within 72 hours of
execution, the will contained shaky signatures, and was
not validly proved as provided under Section 69 of the

--- Page 162 ---
4
Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
12. Consequently, the High Court ruled that upon the
intestate demise of Thiruvenkadam Pillai, his undivided
1/2 share devolved equally, by succession, upon his son
Defendant No. 1 (1/4th share) and daughter Plantiff No. 1
(1/4th share). Hence, a preliminary decree for partition
for 1/4th share and mesne profits was passed in favour of
Plaintiff No. 1 and upon her death, her 1/4 th share
devolved upon Plaintiff No. 2 to Plaintiff No. 10.
13. Aggrieved by the High Court granting a 1/4th share to
the Plaintiffs, the Defendants in the suit have preferred
Civil Appeal Nos. 10358-10361/2010. Aggrieved by the High
Court granting only a 1/4th share instead of the 1/2 share
claimed in the plaint, the Plaintiffs in the suit have
preferred Civil Appeal No. 5566/2014.
14. We have heard the learned Senior counsel appearing
for the appellants and the respondents. We have also
perused the impugned judgment. 
15. Upon perusing the impugned judgment, we are of the
considered  view  that  the  High  Court  has  rightly
disbelieved the registered Will dated 01.02.1963 (Ex.
B46) relied upon by the appellants in Civil Appeal Nos.
10358-10361/2010, who were the Defendants before the
Trial Court, and has correctly fixed the shares as 1/4 th
accruing to the Plaintiffs in the suit and 3/4 th accruing
to the Defendants in the suit.

--- Page 163 ---
5
16. In such view of the matter, we find no reason to
interfere with the impugned judgment.
17. Accordingly, the appeals stand dismissed.
18. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION  
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.3374 OF 2026 
 
SATYA NARAYAN MEHER AND    APPELLANTS 
ANOTHER  
VERSUS 
STATE OF ODISHA             RESPONDENT 
J U D G M E N T 
ATUL S. CHANDURKAR, J 
1. In this criminal appeal, t he appellants challenge their 
conviction for the offence punishable under Section 325 read with 
Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 1. The appellants have 
been sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year 
and to pay a fine of ₹20,000/- each, in default, to further undergo 
rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months each. The fine 
amount has been directed to be disbursed to the widow of the 
victim as compensation.  
2. Facts giving rise to the present prosecution are that on 
19.08.1994 at about 05.30 P.M, a written report was submitted by 
 
1 For short, ‘the Penal Code’ 

--- Page 167 ---
Criminal Appeal No.3374 of 2026  Page 2 of 7 
 
Urmila Meh er-PW1, in which it was stated that her husband 
Chintamani had been assaulted by the appellants along with one 
another, who has since expired.  Chintamani received various 
injuries on his body and it was stated that he had been assaulted 
by means of a spade as well as tangias. He was given first aid and 
thereafter, admitted to hospital. He, however, succumbed to his 
injuries on 22.08.1994. After completion of investigation , all the 
three accused were charged for having committed the offence 
punishable under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Penal 
Code.  
3. Before the Sessions Court, the prosecution examined seven 
witnesses while the defence examined two witnesses. The Sessions 
Court found that despite enmity between the accused and the 
deceased, there was no pre -meditation for causing death of 
Chintamani. Out of the four injuries sustained by the victim, three 
were simple while one injury was grievous in nature. The death 
having occurred due to myocardial infraction, the Sessions Court 
held the accused guilty under Section 304 Part II read with Section 
34 of the Penal Code. They were, accordingly, sentenced to 
rigorous imprisonment for a period of five years each.  

--- Page 168 ---
Criminal Appeal No.3374 of 2026  Page 3 of 7 
 
4. On appeal by the appellants before the High Court of Odisha2, 
the learned Single Judge by his judgment dated 12.02.2026 
recorded a finding that the death of Chintamani was not homicidal 
in nature. The appellants were, therefore, convicted under Section 
325 read with Section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced to 
undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year. They were 
also ordered to pay a fine of ₹20,000/- each, which amount was to 
be disbursed to the widow of Chinta mani as compensation under 
Section 357 of the Code of Criminal Procedure , 1973 3. Being 
aggrieved, the appellants have challenged their conviction. The 
proceedings against accused No.3 abated during pendency of the 
appeal before the High Court. 
5. Ms. Renuka Sahu, learned counsel appearing for the 
appellants assailed the conviction of the appellants by submitting 
that the same was based on weak and hearsay evidence. It was 
submitted that PW3  who was stated to be an eye-witness had 
turned hostile . The other witnesses examined were family 
members of the deceased and were, thus, interested witnesses. The 
other evidence on record was not sufficient to sustain the 
 
2 For short, ‘the High Court’ 
3 For short, ‘the Code’ 

--- Page 169 ---
Criminal Appeal No.3374 of 2026  Page 4 of 7 
 
conviction of the appellants. Moreover, the death having occurred 
due to myocardial infraction and there being no finding tha t the 
injuries caused led to the death of Chinta mani, the appellants 
could not have been so convicted. 
 Without prejudice to the aforesaid, it was submitted that the 
appellant No.1 is now aged sixty-nine years while the appellant 
No.2 is aged fifty-nine years. The incident occurred on 19.08.1994 
and a period of almost thirty-two years have since elapsed. The 
appellants had already undergone incarceration for a period of six 
months and hence, at this point of time , the appellants d id not 
deserve to be required to undergo the remaining sentence. Instead, 
it was submitted that the fine amount could be enhanced so as to 
further compensate the widow of Chintamani. It was, thus, prayed 
that discretion under Article 136 of the Constitution of India be  
accordingly exercised. 
6. Per contra, Ms. Pracheta Kar, learned counsel appearing for 
the respondent su pported the conviction of the appellants. She 
submitted that the evidence on record having been minutely 
examined by the High Court and the conviction of the appellants 
having been altered to one under Section 325 of the Penal Code, 
no interference with the same was called for. Merely because some 

--- Page 170 ---
Criminal Appeal No.3374 of 2026  Page 5 of 7 
 
witnesses were related to the deceased, the same could not be a 
reason to discard their testimonies. In fact, said witnesses 
corroborated with each other and were, thus, reliable. It was, thus, 
submitted that there was no merit in the appeal and it deserved 
dismissal. 
7. We have heard the learned counsel for the parties at length 
and with their assistance, we have  also gone through the records 
of the case. Insofar as the conviction of the appellants under 
Section 325 read with Section 34 of the Penal Code is concerned, 
in our view, the same does not call for any interference. The 
evidence on record, especially the depositions of PW1 and PW4 are 
consistent and there is no reason to disbelieve them merely on the 
ground that they were related to Chinta mani. We find that the 
appreciation of their evidence by the High Court is appropriate and 
there is no reason , whatsoever, to take a different view of the 
matter. Further, the conclusion that the death of Chintamani was 
not homicidal, has not been challenged by the prosecution. We, 
therefore, find that the High Court has assigned sufficient reasons 
for altering the conviction of the appellants from Section 304 Part 
II to Section 325 read with Section 34 of the Penal Code. The 
conviction of the appellants , therefore,  does not warrant 

--- Page 171 ---
Criminal Appeal No.3374 of 2026  Page 6 of 7 
 
interference. 
8. The appellants have been sentenced to undergo rigorous 
imprisonment for a period of one year. The sentence undergone by 
them is six months. The offence under Section 325 of the Penal 
Code is punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine. 
There is no minimum sentence prescribed. The incident leading to 
the prosecution occurred on 19.08.1994. Though the appellants 
were convicted by the Sessions Court vide judgment dated 
08.08.1995, their appeal  before the High Court was pending for 
almost thirty years. The appellant No.1 is now aged sixty-nine 
years while appellant No.2 is aged fifty-nine years. In our view, 
considering the aforesaid aspects and the  backdrop in which the 
unfortunate incident leading to the death of Chintamani occurred 
coupled with the fact that the appellants and the family members 
of Chintamani are distantly related, we are of the view that while 
maintaining the conviction of the appellants under Section 325 
read with Section 34 of the Penal Code, the sentence imposed can 
be partly modified. 
Accordingly, the sentence of imprisonment is reduced to the 
period already undergone by them, which is six months. However, 
the fine amount imposed is enhanced to ₹40,000/- each. The 

--- Page 172 ---
Criminal Appeal No.3374 of 2026  Page 7 of 7 
 
amount of fine shall be disbursed to the widow of Chinta mani or 
her legal representatives as compensation under Section 357 of 
the Code. The amount of the fine shall be deposited by the 
appellants before the Sessions Court, Balangir within a period of 
four weeks from today. On such deposit, the said amount shall be 
disbursed to the widow of Chinta mani or her legal heirs with the 
assistance of the District Legal Ser vices Authorit y, Balangir . 
Failure to deposit the amount of fine would require the appellants 
to undergo the remaining sentence as ordered by the High Court. 
The impugned judgment of the High Court in CRA No.253 of 1995 
dated 12.02.2026 is modified to the aforesaid extent. The Criminal 
Appeal is partly allowed in aforesaid terms.  Pending interlocutory 
application is also disposed of.

1. The present Civil Appeals arise out of the judgment

Forces Tribunal (Regional Bench), Chandigarh (“the AFT”).
2. The Original Applications arose out of challenges to
the amendments introduced vis-à-vis the Regulations for
the Medical Services of the Armed Forces by the Ministry
of Defence on 14.10.1996 (“1996 Policy”). By virtue of
that  amendment,  in  brief,  medical  treatment  for  ex-
servicemen  (and/or  their  dependents)  at  Armed  Forces
Hospitals was conditioned on the ex-serviceman concerned
drawing some form of pensionary benefit. The Respondents
challenged  the  policy  before  the  AFT  vide  the
aforementioned Original Applications. The AFT allowed the
challenges vide the aforementioned judgments and final

--- Page 174 ---

orders, in essence, entitling ex-servicemen (and/or their

Aggrieved by the AFT’s decisions, the Union of India has
come up in appeal before this Court.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. These petitions, filed under Article 32 of the Constitution of
India, seek the intervention of this Court regarding numerous
incidents of violence that occurred during recent protests by
3

--- Page 183 ---
demonstrators, predominantly students, at Jantar Mantar, New Delhi,
and other locations within Delhi. Furthermore, these disturbances
subsequently spread to various other states, including Maharashtra,
Bihar, Assam, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, and
Kerala. In essence, the allegations contended are that violations
have  been  committed  in  violation  of  the  Fundamental  Rights
guaranteed under Articles 14, 19, 21, and 22 of the Constitution of
India, despite the fact that the protesting students were motivated
by concerns over the leakage of question papers pertaining to the
NEET examination 2026. The petitioners have placed on record a
multitude of instances alleging the indiscriminate and excessive
use of force by the police in the National Capital Territory of
Delhi, which includes lathi charge, deployment of pellet guns, and
the use of tear gas, among other measures. The nature of the
incidents detailed in this collection of petitions suggests that:
(i) Pellet guns were used that led to injuries to the young
students, including one boy allegedly losing his eyesight;
(ii) Rubber bullets were used that caused injuries to various
persons, including a woman.
(iii) Electronic batons were used to disperse the crowd.
(iv)  Lathis embedded with nails were also used resulting in
permanent injury and life-threatening injuries to some of the
protestors.
(v) Even a member of the media was assaulted, leading to the
individual sustaining serious injuries.
2. The  violence  allegedly  was  also  perpetrated  by  police
4

--- Page 184 ---
personnel in police and civilian dress, among other instances. At
this stage, we may also briefly consider the opposing account
provided by some of the learned counsel representing the injured
police personnel or their family members. Similar allegations were
made by them, asserting that protestors or certain anti-social
elements who entered the protest site engaged in stone throwing and
other  acts  of  violence,  thereby  inflicting  multiple  serious
injuries on police personnel while they were performing their
duties. Photographs, footage recordings, and other evidence of such
incidents of violence have also been placed on record.
3. Learned Solicitor General of India, representing the Union of
India and NCT of Delhi, at the outset, stated that they have no
objection to an independent and fair probe, as proposed by this
Court to be held in the instances of violence. However, they firmly
denied that any excesses were committed by the police. The Learned
Solicitor  General  further  assailed  that  there  were  hardened
criminals and undesirable elements who had infiltrated the protest
site and engaged in violence against police personnel, resulting in
serious injuries to over 280 officers.
4. Be that as it may, the allegations made by the petitioners,
prima facie, establish a compelling case for an independent and
impartial investigation into the incidents of violence. Such an
investigation will adequately addres s the allegations presented by
the family members of the police personnel, as well as the issues
raised by the learned Solicitor General of India.
5. However, prior to issuing any such order based on a tentative
opinion, we consider it appropriate, in the interest of justice, to
5

--- Page 185 ---
afford a brief period to the NCT of Delhi and the Union of India to
submit their respective versions through an affidavit accompanied
by relevant material. Likewise, we find it necessary to grant a
short hearing to the various States where similar acts of violence
have  occurred,  as  the  proposed  investigation  will  encompass
inquiries into such incidents within those States as well.
6. Consequently, we issue notice to the Chief Secretaries of the
States of Maharashtra, Bihar, Assam, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh,
West Bengal and Kerala. Their Advocate Generals or respective
Standing Counsel (s) shall appear online on the date fixed.
7. Dasti, in addition, is permitted.
8. As an interim measure, we deem it appropriate to issue the
following directions:
(i) Although it has already been stated at the bar by the learned
Solicitor General of India, on instructions, we also, as an
abundant precaution, direct that all CCTV footage, drone footage,
body-worn camera recordings, videography, wireless communication
records, and PCR lodge collections related to the students' protest
be preserved.
(ii) The respondent(s) and police authorities shall ensure that the
personal information and digital data of the protestors, collected
during the students' protests, are preserved and are not disclosed
to the public domain for the time being.
(iii) The respondent(s) may not publish any public data/details of
the protestors, especially students.
(iv) The NCT of Delhi and other States may proceed with the
investigation of the FIRs registered; however, no coercive measures
6

--- Page 186 ---
shall be taken against the protesting students. Such protection,
nonetheless, shall not be extended to the persons with criminal
antecedents.
(v) All States are hereby instructed to release children under the
age of 18, who have been reported to be arrested or detained in
connection with the ongoing protests and who do not possess any
criminal  antecedents.  If  necessary,  these  children  shall  be
released upon the execution of a simple bond by themselves or their
family members, especially if such a requirement is insisted upon
for surety.
9. Post these matters for further consideration on 03.08.2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL  NO.       OF 2026
(@ SLP(CRL.) No.4611/2026)
  DIRECTORATE OF ENFORCEMENT                         APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
RAJNISH BANSAL                                     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. This appeal has been filed by the appellant being aggrieved by
the judgment dated 25.11.2025 under challenge, whereunder the
respondent has been granted anticipatory bail by way of a very
lengthy order having been passed by the High Court. 
3. Learned ASG, appearing on behalf of the appellant, would
submit that the respondent is an absconding accused and a
proclamation  under  Section  82  of  the  Code  of  Criminal
Procedure, 1973 has been issued already. It is a case of
siphoning off of scores of substantial amount of scholarship
funds for marginalized students, meant to be used for a
laudable objective. Fabricated and bogus records have been
created  and  claims  have  been  made  on  that  basis.  The
respondent, even in his statement under Section 50 of the
Prevention of Money Laundering Act (for short, ‘the PMLA’),
has admitted that the records have been fabricated under his
supervision. The High Court was wrong in holding that the

--- Page 206 ---
2
investigation under the PMLA has been fast-tracked only after
the  arrest  of  the  officer  who  was  in-charge  of  the
investigation earlier. The materials filed, as indicated in
the counter affidavit before the High Court, have not been
taken  into  consideration.  Considering  the  nature  of
allegations, the custodial interrogation of the respondent is
very much required. It is further submitted that the action
taken against the earlier officer involved will have no
bearing in the present case. 
4. Mr. Rohatgi, learned senior counsel and Mr. Diwan, learned
senior counsel appearing for the respondent would submit that
the ECIR has been registered way back in the year 2019. The
respondent  has  been  cooperating  with  the  investigation,
pursuant to the summons issued by the appellant. Things have
been fast-tracked at the instance of the appellant only after
the arrest of their earlier Investigation Officer. A higher
officer has also been arrested in some other case. Even
thereafter, the respondent has responded to some of the
summons and could not appear on some other dates for the
reason that no notice has been issued to him. Considering the
facts governing, and also by taking note of the judgment under
challenge wherein, the High Court has considered all the
relevant material, there is no need for any interference with
the impugned order. 
5. Having heard the parties, we are dealing with a case where
serious allegations have been made against the respondent and

--- Page 207 ---
3
co-accused. It is a case of creation of false and bogus claims
and receipt of money running into crores, which was meant for
the welfare of marginalized students. The brother of the
respondent, who was allegedly involved in committing the said
offence along with him, filed an anticipatory bail application
earlier which has been dismissed by the High Court. The
Special  Leave  Petition  filed  has  also  been  dismissed.
Thereafter, he was taken into custody and granted regular
bail. Insofar as the respondent is concerned, the complaint
under the PMLA could not be filed as he was not appearing
before the appellant pursuant to the summons issued, and
cooperating with the investigation. 
6. As rightly submitted by learned ASG, mere arrest of the
appellant’s officer will not enure to the benefit of the
respondent. One has to see the nature of allegations and the
need for custodial interrogation.  As stated earlier, the
allegations against the respondent are serious. It is not as
if  there  are  no  materials  available  to  implicate  the
respondent. The reasoning of the High Court, in our considered
view, cannot be sustained in the eye of law. The High Court
has, in fact, returned a judgment by holding the appellant
liable for malice in law. Having perused the records, we do
not find any malice in law or fact involved in this case,
particularly, when we are dealing with a case of anticipatory
bail. Suffice it to state that considering the nature of
allegations, the custodial interrogation of the respondent is

--- Page 208 ---
4
very much required. 
7. In such view of the matter, we are not inclined to give our
imprimatur  to  the  decision  rendered  by  the  High  Court.
Accordingly, the impugned order stands set aside.  
8. The respondent shall surrender before the appellant within a
period of four weeks from the date of receipt of a copy of
this order.  However, we make it clear that the observations
made  herein  will  have  no  bearing  on  the  regular  bail
application which may be filed by the respondent, and the same
shall be decided on its own merits. 
9. The appeal stands allowed, accordingly,
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

       ………………………………………………………………………J.

NEW DELHI;

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).         OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NO(S).9747 OF 2026)
RAGHUVIR SINGH                                  APPELLANT
VERSUS
STATE OF RAJASTHAN                             RESPONDENT
O R D E R
Leave granted.
This appeal challenges the judgment and
order dated 30.04.2026 passed by the High Court of
Judicature for Rajasthan Bench at Jaipur in S.B.
Criminal 2nd Bail Application No.6053 of 2026.
The appellant herein has been booked for
the crime registered pursuant to FIR No.670/2016
dated 08.11.2016 lodged with  Police Station Bajaj
Nagar,  District  Jaipur  East  with  respect  to
offences punishable under Sections 406, 420, 467,
468, 471 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
(“IPC”).
An application seeking regular bail having
been rejected by the High Court  vide impugned
order  dated  30.04.2026,  the  appellant  has
preferred the instant appeal.
1

--- Page 242 ---
This Court vide its order dated 27.05.2026,
issued notice in the instant matter.
Heard learned counsel for the appellant in
support of the appeal and learned counsel for the
repsondent-State,  and  perused  the  material  on
record. 
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted
that  the  appellant  has  been  in  jail  since
09.10.2025, whereas the other co-accused have been
granted the relief of regular bail; further the
First  Information  Report  is  dated  08.11.2016
whereas no investigation was done for several
years  and  on  09.10.2025  the  appellant  was
apprehended.  Learned counsel for the appellant
further submitted that the allegation against the
appellant and the other co-accused are essentially
arising out of a contract with regard to sale of
plots; that they are civil disputes which have
been  given  a  criminal  colour.  Hence,  on  the
principle of parity, the appellant also may be
granted  the  relief  of  bail  subject  to  the
conditions to be imposed by this Court.
Per contra, learned counsel for the first
2

--- Page 243 ---
respondent-State as well as learned counsel for
the Complainant opposed the grant of relief to the
appellant herein by contending that the appellant
was absconding for several years and therefore, no
action could be taken although the FIR is dated
08.11.2016. It may be that the co-accused have
been granted the relief of bail, but any relief to
be granted to the appellant would jeopardize the
trial of the case. In the circumstances, they
submitted that the appeal may be dismissed.
Considering the facts on record, in our
view, the case for bail is made out.
We, therefore, allow this appeal and direct
as under:
“The appellant shall be produced before
the concerned trial Court as early as possible
and the trial Court shall release him on bail,
subject to such conditions as it may deem
appropriate to impose to ensure his presence
in the proceedings arising out of FIR No.
670/2016 mentioned above.”
It is directed that the appellant shall
extend complete cooperation in the trial of the
instant case. 
The appellant shall not misuse his liberty
in any manner.
3

--- Page 244 ---
Any infraction of the conditions may entail
cancellation  of  the  bail  granted  to  the
appellant.
With  these  observations,  the  appeal  is
allowed.
………………………………………………………, J
       (B.V. NAGARATHNA)
…………………………………………………………, J
(R.MAHADEVAN)

JULY 28, 2026

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).            OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NO(S).9857 OF 2026)
ARIF ANSARI                                   APPELLANT
VERSUS
THE STATE OF JHARKHAND                       RESPONDENT
O R D E R
Leave granted.
This appeal challenges the judgment and
order dated 11.05.2026 passed by the High Court
of Jharkhand at Ranchi, in B.A No.2628 of 2026.
The appellant has been facing trial in
connection with a crime registered pursuant to
FIR No.42 of 2025 dated 24.05.2025 lodged with
Police Station Cyber Crime, District Jamtara in
respect of offences punishable under Sections
111(2)(b),  111(3),  111(4),  317(2),  317(5),
318(4), 319(2), 336(3), 338, 340(2) read with
Section 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023 (“BNS”, in short) and Sections 42(3)(e) of
the Telecommunications Act and Sectins 66(B),
66(C), 66(D) of the I.T.Act.
The  application  seeking  regular  bail
1

--- Page 248 ---
having been rejected by the High Court  vide
impugned order dated 11.05.2026, the appellant
has preferred the instant appeal.
This  Court,  vide its  order  dated
27.05.2026, issued notice in the instant matter.
Heard learned counsel for the appellant
in support of the appeal and learned counsel for
the respondent-State and perused the material on
record.
Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant
submitted that the appellant has been in jail
since 24.05.2025, although the other co-accused
have been granted either regular bail or even
anticipatory bail. He therefore submitted that
on the principle of parity the appellant also
may be granted the similar relief. He also
submitted that five out of twenty four witnesses
have been examined and there is every likelihood
of delay in the conclusion of the trial. In the
circumstances, the impugned order may be set
aside and the relief of bail may be granted to
the appellant subject to the conditions imposed
by this Court.
2

--- Page 249 ---
Per contra, learned counsel appearing for
the  respondent-State  with  reference  to  the
counter-affidavit, contended that since recovery
of  three  mobile  phones  were  made  from  the
appellant herein, there is concrete evidence as
against him; that any relief to be granted to
the  appellant  herein  may  jeopardize  and
frustrate  the  trial.  In  the  circumstances,
learned counsel contended that there is no merit
in this appeal and the same may be dismissed.
Considering the facts on record, in our
view, the case for regular bail is made out.
We,  therefore,  allow  this  appeal  and
direct as under:
“The appellant shall be produced
before the concerned Trial Court as early
as  possible  and  the  Trial  Court  shall
release  him  on  bail,  subject  to  such
conditions as it may deem appropriate to
impose  to  ensure  his  presence  in  the
proceedings arising out of FIR No.42 of
2025 mentioned above.”
It is directed that the appellant shall
extend complete cooperation in the trial of the
instant case. 
3

--- Page 250 ---
The  appellant  shall  not  misuse  his
liberty in any manner.
Any  infraction  of  the  conditions  may
entail  cancellation  of  bail  granted  to  the
appellant.
With these observations, the appeal is
allowed.

    (B.V. NAGARATHNA)
………………………………………………………, J

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.   3447   OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 9798/2026)
UGRASEN SINGH GAUTAM      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of  Madhya
Pradesh.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 13.10.2025
passed by the High court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
prayer for anticipatory bail of the appellant.
4. It is stated that appellant is apprehending his
arrest in connection with Crime No.125/2018 registered at
Police Station- Sukhi Sevaniya, District- Bhopal, Madhya
Pradesh under Section 34(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Excise
Act, 1915 (as amended).
5. The prosecution case is that following a search
carried  out,  756  litres  of  country  made  liquor  was
recovered  from  a  truck;  the  truck  driver  later  on
1

--- Page 274 ---
confessed that he was carrying the liquor from Orissa to
be handed over to the appellant.
6. This Court by order dated 19.06.2026 had issued
notice and granted interim protection to the appellant
subject  to  the  appellant  co-operating  with  the
investigation.
7. In the hearing today, on a query, learned counsel for
the appellant submits that though appellant has written to
the Investigating Officer, he has not yet been summoned in
connection with the investigation of the aforesaid case.
8. Opposing the prayer for anticipatory bail, learned
counsel for the respondent-State of Madhya Pradesh submits
that involvement of the appellant is quite apparent. He
has been evading investigation all this while. There is a
previous criminal antecedent of the appellant, though not
under the Madhya Pradesh Excise Act. He further submits
that the offence carries a maximum sentence of 03 years
upon conviction.
9. Upon hearing learned counsel for the parties and on
due consideration, we are of the view that the order dated
19.06.2026 passed by this Court is required to be made
absolute.
10. That being the position, we set aside the impugned
order dated 13.10.2025 passed by the High Court and make
the  order  dated  19.06.2026  absolute.  We  direct  the
appellant to appear before the Investigating Officer on
04.08.2026 at 11:00 AM and on any subsequent date(s) as
2

--- Page 275 ---
may be fixed by the Investigating Officer.
11. Consequently, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

this  petition  and  had  passed  an  order
whereby Conditions (h) and (i) were stayed
and  in  respect  of  Condition  (a),  the
appellant was granted additional time to
1

--- Page 284 ---
make deposit of the balance 25 per cent so
as to make the total deposit equivalent to

“1.  The  petitioner  is  impugning
Conditions (c),(h) and (i) imposed in
the bail granting order. It is the
case of the petitioner that he had
expressed willingness to deposit 50
per cent of the amount in question
with the learned trial court to show
his bona fides without prejudice to
his  rights  and  contentions  whereas
the  High  Court  had  directed  vide
Condition  No.  (c)  to  deposit  the
entire balance amount remaining after
depositing the initial 25 per cent
amount. In such circumstances, it is
submitted  that  Condition  No.  (c)
needs to be deleted from the bail
granting order.
2. As regards Conditions (h) and (i),
it is stated that these are onerous
conditions  as  the  movement  of  the
2

--- Page 285 ---
petitioner  within  the  country  is
restricted.
3. Issue notice, returnable in six
weeks.

noticed above, we are of the view
that  instead  of  depositing  the
remaining amount, after deposit of 25
per cent as per Condition (a), the
petitioner  shall  deposit  the
remaining 25 per cent amount so as to
make the total deposit 50 per cent.
The remaining 25 per cent shall be
deposited  within  four  weeks  from
today.
5. Insofar as Conditions (h) and (i)
are  concerned,  they  shall  remain
stayed.” 
6. It is not in dispute that the balance
25 per cent has been deposited in terms of
this Court’s order.
7. Insofar as Conditions (h) and (i),
which have been stayed by our interim order
dated 23.03.2026, are concerned, we are of
3

--- Page 286 ---
the  view  that  since  the  appellant  has

from the country is remote.

justification for imposition of Conditions
(h) and (I), as recorded in the order dated
24.12.2025 of the High Court.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
EXTRAORDINARY CRIMINAL JURISDICTION
SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NOS. 11234-11235/2026
KRSKA BUILDERS LLP ..... PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
PUNEET AGRAWAL & ORS. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Challenge in these special leave petitions is to the interim
orders dated 20.05.2026 and 21.05.2026 passed by a learned
Judge  of  the  High  Court  of  Uttarakhand  at  Nainital  in
Criminal Writ Petition No. 762/2026.
2. We may note that two writ petitions were before the learned
Judge,  viz.  Criminal  Writ  Petition  Nos.  1431/2026  and
762/2026.  We may further note that the learned Judge had
appeared as a counsel for Prateek Resorts & Builders Private
Limited, the predecessor-in-interest of KRSKA Builders LLP,
the petitioner herein, in WPMS No. 1478/2013 and we are
informed that the land involved in the said case was the very
same land which is the subject matter of enquiry before the
learned Judge and in relation to which the impugned interim
orders  were  passed.  It  appears  that  Prateek  Resorts  &
Builders Private Limited filed an application before the
1

--- Page 294 ---
SLP(Crl.) Nos. 11234-11235/2026
learned Judge seeking to be impleaded and the same is still
pending consideration. 
3. In such circumstances, in the interest of judicial propriety,
the learned Judge ought not to have entertained and passed
orders in the matter. Trite to state, justice must not only
be done but must also be seen to be done. Passing orders
either in favour of or against a former client, a private
entity, does not further that cause. 
4. That apart, we may also note that the writ petitions filed
before the learned Judge were on altogether different issues
and the scope of those writ petitions has been enlarged by
the learned Judge by way of the impugned interim orders.
Even if such an exercise was taken up with the best of
intentions, it was not proper for the learned Judge to do so
in writ petitions which had nothing to do with the issues
sought to be addressed. In the event the learned Judge was of
the opinion that this was a matter that required to be
espoused in the cause of public interest, appropriate steps
could have been taken by placing the matter before the Public
Interest Litigation Committee constituted in the High Court
or by referring the matter to the Hon’ble The Chief Justice
of the High Court for necessary measures to be taken in
accordance with due procedure.  
5. However, as the learned Judge has already passed certain
orders which are presently holding the field and as it
2

--- Page 295 ---
SLP(Crl.) Nos. 11234-11235/2026
appears that undertakings have also been given with regard to
not cutting down trees, we are not inclined to interfere with
the said orders or undertakings at this stage.  It is for the
appropriate Bench of the High Court, as and when it takes up
the matter, to go into all aspects on facts and in law,
including the validity of the orders impugned presently.  All
issues are left open to be addressed before the said Bench.
6. This order shall be communicated to the Hon’ble The Chief
Justice of the High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital for
taking suitable steps with regard to the listing of Criminal
Writ  Petition  Nos.  762/2026  and  1431/2026  as  well  as
initiation of a public interest litigation, if warranted.
7. With the above observations, the special leave petitions are
disposed of.
      Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.   1392     OF 2026  
JAYKANT      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and  
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent -State  of  Madhya  
Pradesh.
2. Appellant was initially convicted by the Trial Court  
under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for  
short, ‘IPC’) and sentenced to undergo Imprisonment for  
Life. On appeal, the High Court altered the conviction  
from one under Section 302 of IPC to one under Section 304 
Part-II of IPC. The sentence of Life Imprisonment was  
accordingly modified to Rigorous Imprisonment (for short,  
‘R.I.’) of 05 years and a fine of Rs.5,000/-, with a  
default stipulation.
3. When the appellant approached this Court assailing  
the order of the High Court, this Court by order dated  
03.03.2025 issued notice limited to quantum of sentence.  
It was clarified that the notice was issued subject to  
appellant depositing a sum of Rs.5,00,000/- with the Trial 
Court.
4. In the proceeding held on 23.05.2025, this Court  
1

--- Page 309 ---
recorded that appellant had deposited the aforesaid amount 
of Rs.5,00,000/-. On 11.08.2025, this Court after noticing 
that appellant had deposited the amount of Rs.5,00,000/-  
observed that appellant should deposit a further amount of 
Rs.7,00,000/- with the Trial Court, thus making a total of 
Rs.12,00,000/-, to compensate the victim’s family.
5. On 16.12.2025, it was submitted before this Court by  
learned counsel for the appellant that appellant is not in 
a position to make a further deposit of Rs.7,00,000/-;  
instead  Rs.3,00,000/-  was  deposited  in  place  of  
Rs.7,00,000/-.
6. On 09.03.2026, this Court granted leave.
7. Today, learned counsel for the appellant submits that  
on 30.09.2025, appellant would complete the sentence of 05 
years including remission. The appellant is a daily wage  
earning labourer. Payment of such huge amount is not  
possible for him; anyway, the full sentence imposed on him 
is nearing the end. Therefore, he has instructions not to  
pursue the appeal.
8. Learned counsel for the respondent-State of Madhya  
Pradesh submits that the fact remains that appellant could 
not deposit the entire amount as directed by this Court.
9. We have considered the rival submissions made at the  
Bar and perused the materials on record.
10. The sentence imposed on the appellant, as modified by  
the  High  Court,  is  R.I.  for  05  years  and  fine  of 
Rs.5,000/-, with a default stipulation.
2

--- Page 310 ---
11. This Court, with a view to compensate the victim,  
initially directed payment of Rs.5,00,000/- subject to  
which notice was issued. When this Court observed that  
appellant should pay further amount, he expressed his  
inability to pay so, considering his economic condition  
and instead deposited a sum of Rs.3,00,000/-. Learned  
counsel submits that notwithstanding his poor financial  
condition, he has deposited a sum of Rs.8,00,000/- only  
with the hope that his matter would be heard by this Court 
and that his sentence of imprisonment would be reduced.  
That is not a possibility now as the entire sentence would 
be over shortly. In such circumstances, appellant may be  
directed to withdraw the Criminal Appeal as well as the  
amount deposited before the Trial Court.
12. We are of the view that the family members of the  
deceased are entitled to compensation as per the scheme  
that may have been prepared by the State in terms of  
Section 357A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (for  
short, ‘CrPC’). If the family members have not done so, we 
direct the District Legal Services Authority, Jabalpur,  
Madhya  Pradesh  to  assist  the  family  members  of  the 
deceased to avail such compensation.
13. We are also of the view that the deposit made by the  
appellant before the Trial Court, i.e. Rs.8,00,000/-,  
should be refunded back to him because such deposit is  
beyond the punishment imposed on him.
14. Accordingly,  while  permitting  the  appellant  to  
3

--- Page 311 ---
withdraw the Criminal Appeal, we direct that the Trial  
Court, i.e. Court of Special Judge, the Scheduled Castes & 
Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, Jabalpur, 
shall refund the amount of Rs.8,00,000/- deposited by the  
appellant within a period of six weeks from today.
15. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is disposed of as  
withdrawn.
16. A copy of this order be forthwith sent to the Member  
Secretary, Madhya Pradesh Legal Services Authority to do  
the needful.
17. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed  
of.
…………………………………………………...J.
      
   [UJJAL BHUYAN]
…………………………………………………...J.
     [ATUL S. CHANDURKAR]
NEW DELHI;
24th JULY, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF S.L.P. (CRL.) NO. 17918 OF 2025)
ABDUL JAFFER                             ...Appellant
VERSUS
ASSISTANT DIRECTOR OF ENFORCEMENT         ...Respondent
 O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant has been charged for the offences
punishable under Sections 3 and 4 read with Section 70
of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (for
short, ‘the PMLA’) in connection with Enforcement Case
Information  Report  bearing  No.ECIR/NGSZO/09/2020.  The
bail application preferred by the appellant was rejected
by the Trial Court, the appellant approached the High
Court of Judicature at Bombay for grant of bail, which
was also rejected by the High Court vide impugned order
dated 10.10.2025. Aggrieved, the appellant is before us.
3. We have heard the learned Senior counsel appearing
for the appellant and the learned Additional Solicitor
General appearing for the respondent.
4. The sum and substance of the allegations against
1

--- Page 330 ---
the  appellant  is  that  he  has  orchestrated  illicit
exports of red sanders valuing to the tune of Rs.63.64
crores.
5. On a previous occasion while adjourning the matter,
considering the nature of allegations, we have issued a
direction to the Trial Court to conclude the recording
of pre-charge evidence. The learned counsel appearing
for the appellant submits that apart from the fact that
the appellant has been in custody for a period of about
one year and two months, the recording of pre-charge
evidence is yet to begin as per the affidavit  filed on
behalf of the respondent.  
6. From the submissions made, we do not find any
wilful attempt made on the part of the respondent to
conclude the recording of the pre-charge evidence.  In
fact, substantial efforts have to be made only on the
part of the respondent.  Suffice it is to state that the
appellant has been in custody for about one year and two
months.  
7. In view of the above, we are inclined to set aside
the impugned order dated 10.10.2025 passed by the High
Court. 
2

--- Page 331 ---
8. Accordingly, the impugned order stands set aside and
the  appellant  is  granted  bail  on  such  terms  and
conditions as may be imposed by the concerned Trial
Court. However, we make it clear that the Trial Court
shall comply with the direction issued vide this Court’s
order dated 25.05.2026 within a period of four weeks
from today.
9. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal stands allowed. 
10. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.
………………………………………………………J.
     (M.M. Sundresh)
………………………………………………………J.
     (Prasanna B. Varale)
New Delhi;
July 27, 2026.
