1 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026 
(ARISING OUT OF S.L.P. (C) NO.11623 OF 2026) 
 
SAYARA KHATOON @ SHAYARA KHATOON & ANR.  ...APPELLANTS 
 
 
VERSUS 
 
 
THE STATE OF BIHAR & ORS.       ...RESPONDENTS 
 
 
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted. 
2. The present appeal has been preferred against the 
order of the High Court of Judicature at Patna, whereby 
the request of the appellants for appointment of 
appellant No.2 on compassionate grounds, following the 
death of the husband of appellant No.1 and father of the 
appellant No.2, was rejected.  The rejection was on two 
grounds, namely, the objection raised by the brother of 
appellant No.1 and the policy formulated by the 
Government of Bihar dated 10.12.2014, under which only a 
divorced or deserted daughter is eligible for appointment 
on compassionate grounds. 
3. The learned counsel appearing for the appellants 
submits that the very same brother had earlier furnished 
a no objection certificate.  Thus, the said ground for 
rejection no longer survives.  The other ground for 

--- Page 342 ---
 
2 
rejection, according to the learned counsel is that the 
policy dated 10.12.2014, which restricts compassionate 
appointment to a daughter only if she is divorced or 
deserted.  It is contended that the policy is violative 
of Article 14 of the Constitution of India, 1950. 
4. The learned counsel for the respondent submitted that 
the policy has not been challenged and the rationale 
behind the policy is that a daughter, upon marriage is 
ordinarily expected to leave her parental home.  It was 
further submitted that compassionate appointment is not a 
matter of right and the same is governed by the policy. 
5. This Court has repeatedly held that any 
classification differentiating a daughter from a son is, 
per se, unconstitutional.  On a perusal of the policy, we 
find that classification restricting eligibility only to 
a divorced or deserted daughter cannot be sustained in 
the eye of law.  There cannot be a presumption in law 
that, after marriage, a daughter severs her ties with her 
parental family and resides with husband in her 
matrimonial home.  In the present case, a specific 
statement has been made by the appellant that, although 
her divorce has not been formally recognized by law, she 
has been also living with her parental family.  In fact, 
she has the support of her entire family including her 
mother and brother.  In any event, adopting a hyper-

--- Page 343 ---
 
3 
technical approach cannot be a ground to deny 
consideration of her claim for compassionate appointment, 
the appeal is entitled for consideration on merits.  As 
already stated, the objection of the brother also no 
longer survives. 
6. In view of the above, we are inclined to set aside 
the impugned order and consequently, the order rejecting 
claim for compassionate appointment also stands set 
aside.  The respondent is directed to consider the case 
of the appellant for compassionate appointment on merits 
within a period of eight weeks from the date of receipt 
of a copy of this order. 
7. Accordingly, the Civil Appeal is allowed. 
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed 
of. 
 
………………………………………………………J. 
         (M.M. SUNDRESH)  
 
 
………………………………………………………J. 
          (PRASANNA B. VARALE)  
New Delhi; 
July 23, 2026.

the very same grounds and prayers urged in the present
Review Petition were previously raised by the Review
Petitioner in Miscellaneous Application Nos. 455-462 of
2026, which were filed pursuant to the dismissal of the
aforementioned Civil Appeals. 

--- Page 350 ---
2

“We have heard the learned senior counsel appearing
for the parties.

The Miscellaneous Application(s) stand dismissed
with  the  clarification  that  the  order  dated
06.11.2025  having  been  passed  by  taking  into

of the instant case will have no bearing on any
other matter pertaining to the Rajasthan Sales Tax
Act, 1994 and Rajasthan Value Added Tax Act, 2003.
Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.”
6. As the issues raised herein have already been agitated,
duly  considered,  and  laid  to  rest  with  a  specific
clarification in the prior Miscellaneous Applications,

is wholly misconceived and devoid of merit.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.   3443   OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 9344/2026)
BABLU SAHU & ANR.      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF CHHATTISGARH     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant(s)
and  learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Chhattisgarh.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant(s) are aggrieved by order dated 12.12.2025
passed by the High court of Chhattisgarh (briefly the
‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the regular bail
application of the appellant(s).
4. Appellant is an accused in FIR No.404/2025 registered
at  Police  Station-  Shivrinarayan,  District-  Janjgir-
Champa, Chhattisgarh under Sections 20(b)(ii)(c) and 29 of
the Narcotics Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
(for short, ‘NDPS Act’).
5. Case of the prosecution is that on 14.09.2025, the
police,  acting  on  the  basis  of  secret  information,
intercepted  a  grey  coloured  Ford  Figo  car  bearing
1

--- Page 370 ---
Registration No.CG-10-FA-1143, coming from Deoribhuiya and
proceeding towards Lawan. From the dicky of the vehicle,
22  packets  of  Ganja were  recovered,  whereafter
appellant(s) were taken into custody.
6. On  13.05.2026,  this  Court  had  issue  notice,
whereafter learned counsel for the respondent-State of
Chhattisgarh has filed counter affidavit.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant(s) submits that
appellant(s) are not owners of the vehicle from which the
contraband was seized. He submits that they are in custody
since 14.09.2025, which is more than 10 months. The
investigation is complete and trial has commenced. Health
condition  of  the  father  of  Appellant  No.01  is  also
precarious. As a matter of fact, this Court had directed
the appellant(s) to inform the Court about the present
medical condition of the father of Appellant No.01.
8. Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Chhattisgarh, on the other hand, has referred to the
counter affidavit filed by the respondent and submits that
the medical condition of the father of Appellant No.01 is
not a recent one. Though he is bed-ridden, he has been in
that condition since 2024. That apart, she submits that
the trial is ongoing where 07 witnesses out of 11 have
been examined. Next date fixed is 31.07.2026.
9. Responding to such submission of learned counsel for
the respondent-State of Chhattisgarh, learned counsel for
the petitioner submits that the pace at which the trial is
2

--- Page 371 ---
ongoing, it would not be possible to conclude the trial
expeditiously. In the meanwhile, health of the father of
Appellant No.01 is a matter of concern. There are no
previous antecedents of the appellant(s).
10. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and on
due consideration, we are of the view that a case for
grant  of  bail  to  the  appellant(s)  is  made  out.
Accordingly, the impugned order dated 12.12.2025 passed by
the High Court is set aside.
11. Consequently, we direct that the appellant(s) shall
be produced before the concerned Special Court within a
maximum period of 07 days from today, whereafter they
shall be released on bail on such terms and conditions as
may be deemed appropriate. In addition, the appellant(s)
shall co-operate with the ongoing trial and not seek any
adjournment, except for compelling reasons.
12. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.   3444   OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 7660/2026)
RAJKUMAR DEOKAR      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF CHHATTISGARH     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent-State of Chhattisgarh.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 09.04.2026
passed by the High court of Chhattisgarh (briefly the
‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the regular bail
application of the appellant.
4. Appellant is an accused in FIR No.88/2024 registered
at  Police  Station-  Kotwali,  District-  Rajnandgaon,
Chhattisgarh under Sections 420 and 120B of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’).
5. The  substratum  of  the  allegations  against  the
appellant is that one Rajesh Lunia had approached the bank
for obtaining a gold loan on the basis of certification of
the appellant, who is an approved valuer of the bank. Upon
such certification, the bank had sanctioned a loan of
1

--- Page 374 ---
Rs.48,09,984/-. However, it was later on found that the
gold pledged was not genuine.
6. This Court by order dated 04.05.2026 had issued
notice,  pursuant  to  which  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State  of  Chhattisgarh  has  filed  counter
affidavit.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that he is
in  custody  since  19.01.2026.  Investigation  qua  the
appellant is complete. No recovery has been made from him.
He has no criminal antecedent. Therefore, he may be
enlarged on bail.
8. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent-State
of Chhattisgarh after referring to the counter affidavit
filed by the respondent submits that the main person, who
had availed the loan on the basis of fake gold pledged, is
absconding. Though charge sheet has been filed and charges
have been framed qua the appellant, the trial has not yet
commenced. He submits that if appellant is granted bail at
this stage, it will not only hamper in the apprehension of
the main accused but may also cause delay in the trial.
9. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and on
due consideration, we are of the view that a case for
grant of bail to the appellant is made out, as appellant
cannot be faulted for absconding of the main accused. In
any case, he has been in custody since 19.01.2026. No
recovery has been made from the person or premises of the
appellant. He has got no criminal antecedent.
2

--- Page 375 ---
10. Accordingly,  the  impugned  order  dated  09.04.2026
passed by the High Court is set aside.
11. Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
produced before the concerned Trial Court within a maximum
period of 07 days from today, whereafter he shall be
released on bail on such terms and conditions as may be
deemed appropriate.
12. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

               S U P R E M E  C O U R T  O F  I N D I A
                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) Diary No(s). 32133/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated 12-07-2022  
in CR. MISC. No. 31350/2021 30-08-2025 in CR. MISC. No. 52139/2024  
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Patna]
SHASHIKANT KUMAR                                   Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR & ANR.                          Respondent(s)
(IA No. 176599/2026 - CONDONATION OF DELAY IN FILING
IA No. 176598/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING C/C OF THE IMPUGNED 
JUDGMENT
IA No. 176601/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.)
 
Date : 27-07-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE UJJAL BHUYAN
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE ATUL S. CHANDURKAR
For Petitioner(s): Mr. Manoj Kumar Srivastava, AOR
                   Mr. Akshansh Harsh, Adv.
                   Mr. Alok Ranjan, Adv. 
  
For Respondent(s): Mr. Samir Ali Khan, AOR
                   Mr. Pranjal Sharma, Adv.
                   Mr. Kashif Irshad Khan, Adv. 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard learned counsel for the petitioner  
and learned counsel for the respondent-State of Bihar.
2. Delay condoned.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that  
High Court of Patna at Bihar (briefly the ‘High Court’  
hereinafter)  was  not  justified  in  imposing  the  
condition  of  payment  of  maintenance  amount  of  
Rs.6,000/-  for  the  month  of  July,  2026  to  the  
1

--- Page 386 ---
informant-wife as a condition for granting anticipatory 
bail. In support of this, he has placed reliance on a  
number of decisions of this Court including  Gajanan 
Dattatray Gore versus State of Maharashtra and Another  
[2025 SCC OnLine SC 1571].
4. It is stated that petitioner-husband has been  
arrayed as an accused in FIR No.66 of 2020 registered  
at Police Station- Mahila Thana, District- Nalanda,  
Bihar under Sections 498A, 341, 323, 504, 506 and  
494/34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short,  
‘IPC’).
5. On 12.07.2022, the High Court granted anticipatory 
bail to the petitioner on condition that he should  
furnish bail bond of Rs.10,000/- each with two sureties 
of the like amount to the satisfaction of the Court of  
SDJM, Nalanda at Biharsharif. It was further directed  
that the bail bonds of the petitioner would be accepted 
by the Magistrate on showing receipt of deposit of  
Rs.6,000/- by the petitioner in the account of the  
informant, being the maintenance amount for the month  
of July, 2026. It was clarified that the aforesaid  
payment would be subject to any order passed in the  
maintenance case for final settlement.
6. Petitioner filed an application for modification  
of the aforesaid order dated 12.07.2022. By order dated 
30.08.2025, the High Court declined to modify the  
condition of deposit of maintenance by the petitioner  
2

--- Page 387 ---
in the account of the informant. However, it was  
directed  that  petitioner  shall  furnish  bail  bonds 
subject to deposit of Rs.10,000/- to the concerned  
District Legal Services Authority which should be used  
for the purchase of furniture and beautification of the 
Court premises.
7. In  Gajanan Dattatray Gore , this Court clarified  
and directed as under:
“24. Be that as it may, now we have made  
ourselves very clear that there shall not  
be a single order that the High Courts and  
the Trial Courts shall pass for grant of  
regular bail or anticipatory bail on the  
basis of any accused or his/her family  
members giving an undertaking to deposit a  
particular  amount.  The  plea  shall  be  
decided strictly on merits in accordance  
with law. If the case is made out on merits  
the court may exercise its discretion and  
if no case is made out on merits the court  
shall reject the plea for regular bail or  
anticipatory  bail  as  the  case  may  be.  
However,  in  any  circumstances  the  High  
Courts or trial courts shall not pass a  
conditional  order  of  regular  bail  or  
anticipatory bail.”
8. That being the position, we set aside the orders  
dated 12.07.2022 and 30.08.2025 passed by the High  
3

--- Page 388 ---
Court and remand the matter back to the High Court for  
considering afresh the prayer for anticipatory bail of  
the petitioner in accordance with law.
9. Consequently, Criminal Miscellaneous No.31350 of  
2021 would stand revived. The matter shall be taken up  
by the High Court on 03.08.2026 for fresh consideration 
on merit.
10. Accordingly,  the  Special  Leave  Petition  is  
disposed of.
11. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand  
disposed of.
(ABHINAV KUMAR)                                (CHETNA BALOONI)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal  No(s).  3436/2026
SLP (Crl.) No(s). 10313/2026
NEERAJ MANDIYA                                     Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH                             Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order dated
11.03.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  of
Judicature at Allahabad rejecting the regular
bail prayer of the appellant in connection with
Case Crime No. 61/2025, registered at P.S.
Cyber Crime, District Gautam Bhudh Nagar.
4. The submission of the learned counsel
for  the  appellant  is  that  the  allegations
against  him  are  in  respect  of  opening  an
account and serving it as a mule account for
diversion of funds. It has been submitted that
1

--- Page 394 ---
the offences, for which the appellant has been
indicted,  are  all  triable  by  a  Court  of
Magistrate and by now he has suffered over one
year of pending trial incarceration. There is
no likelihood of trial being concluded in near
future and, therefore, the appellant, who has
no previous criminal antecedents, be released
on bail.
5.  The  learned  Counsel  for  the  State-
respondent has opposed the prayer for bail by
submitting that the funds transferred to the
account are of large magnitude and the account
of the appellant has admittedly been used for
such transfer.
6. Be that as it may, having regard to the
nature of the offences, the fact that they are
triable  by  a  Court  of  Magistrate  and  the
appellant  has  suffered  over  one  year  of
incarceration pending trial, we are of the view
that the appellant is entitled to be released
on bail at this stage.
7.  Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The
order passed by the High Court rejecting the
regular bail prayer of the appellant is set
2

--- Page 395 ---
aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on bail on
such terms and conditions as the trial court
may  deem  fit  to  impose  in  the  facts  and
circumstances  of  the  case.  One  of  the
conditions  so  imposed  shall  require  the
appellant to co-operate in the trial and in the
event of his non-cooperation, his bail bonds
would stand cancelled. 
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

certiorari,  quashing  the  revised  layout  dated  01.05.2023
sanctioned by respondent no.2 on Plot No. 1, Knowledge 04,
Greater NOIDA, Gautam Budh Nagar, U.P.
(iii) Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of mandamus
directing the respondent no.2 and 3 to not allow respondent
no.5/builder to proceed with the construction on Plot No. 1,
Knowledge 04, Greater NOIDA, Gautam Budh Nagar, U.P. in Palm
Olympia Housing Society in contravention of the U.P. Apartment
(Promotion of Construction, Ownership and Maintenance) Act, 2010
and building regulations of Greator Noida Authority/respondent
no.2.
(iv) Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of mandamus
restraining respondent no.5 from proceeding with any construction

--- Page 403 ---
3
which affects the undivided interests of the petitioners in the
common areas, amenities appurtenant to their flats and green
areas in the Palm Olympia Housing Society, Plot No. 1, Knowledge
04, Greater NOIDA, Gautam Budh Nagar, U.P."
4. The High Court declined to entertain the writ petition, saying
that the petitioners (home buyers) have an alternative efficacious
remedy  under  the  U.P.  Apartment  (Promotion  of  Construction,
Ownership and Maintenance) Act, 2010 (for short, 'the Act 2010').
The High Court, while disposing of the writ petition, observed that
the petitioners may invoke the efficacious remedy before the
competent authority under Section 27 of the Act 2010 and Section
41(3) of the U.P. Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973 (for
short, 'the Act 1973').
5. Being dissatisfied with the impugned order passed by the High
Court, the petitioners are here before us.
6. We heard Mr. Jayant Bhushan, the learned Senior Counsel
appearing for the petitioners (home buyers), Mr. Ravindra Kumar,
the learned Senior Counsel appearing for Respondent No. 2, Mr.
V.Giri, the learned Senior Counsel, Dr. Abhishek Manu Singhvi, the
learned Senior Counsel assisted by Mr. Kanu Agarwal, the learned
counsel appearing for the Respondent No. 5  and Mr. Shashank
Shekhar Singh, the learned counsel appearing for the State of U.P.
7. Mr.  Jayant  Bhushan,  appearing  for  the  home  buyers,  has
manifold contentions to raise. According to him, his clients have
been duped by Respondent No. 5. He banks upon the original brochure
and other commitments made by the developer at the relevant point
of time when his client s purchased the flats in the scheme by name
Palm Olympia. It is alleged that the Respondent No.5 has committed
breach of many rules, regulations etc.
8. On the other hand, the learned Senior counsel appearing for
the Developer has also manifold contentions to raise. According to
him, every thing is in accordance with the sanctioned plan.
9. The learned Senior counsel appearing for the Greater Noida
Industrial Development Authority would submit that the plan as put

--- Page 404 ---
4
forward by the Respondent No.5 has been duly sanctioned after
considering all the relevant aspects of the matter.
10. We are of the view that all contentions raised before us along
with all the relevant aspects should be first looked into by the
competent authority of the State Government under the two Acts,
referred to above. The competent authority of the State Government
shall  hear  all  the  stakeholders.  It  shall  be  open  for  the
petitioners as home buyers to put forward their submissions before
the competent authority. The other side may also put forward their
submissions.
11. Let the Competent Authority of the State Government look into
all the relevant aspects of the matter and pass an appropriate
reasoned  order in accordance with law within a period of three
months from today.
12. Any party that may be aggrieved with  the order that may be
passed by the Competent Authority may take appropriate steps to
challenge the same in accordance with law before the appropriate
forum.
13. It goes without saying that any further construction will be
at the risk and peril of the Respondent No.5 and will be subject to
the final orders that may be passed by the Competent Authority.
14. We expect the Competent Authority of the State Government to
give due consideration to all the relevant issues and  pass a
reasoned order after taking into consideration all the submissions
that may be canvassed by each of the parties to this litigation and
if necessary also undertake the spot inspection of the site in
question.
15. With the aforesaid, this petition stands disposed of.
16. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL No.         OF 2026
[SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) No. 14490 OF 2026]
E NARAYANAN                  Appellant(s)
VERSUS
V RAVIKUMAR                           Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. This appeal arises out of the final order dated 26.03.2026
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras in CRP No. 5047 of
2025.
3. The respondent filed a suit for permanent injunction of the suit
property measuring 148 sq. ft., claiming to be the owner of the
property measuring 148 sq. ft. The respondent submits that on 570
sq. ft., a residential building is built and the remaining 148 sq.
ft. has been earmarked as passage for the property to reach the
main road.
4. The defendant filed a written statement and approached the
plaint averment.
5. While the suit was filed on 26.04.2019, the respondent -
plaintiff filed an interlocutory application on 23.07.2025 seeking
amendment  of  the  plaint  to  introduce  a  statement  that  " the
defendant has no right or title to use this suit passage and his
action in using the suit passage (clearly described in the Rough
sketch attached with the plaint) is unauthorised and unsustainable
in law".

--- Page 410 ---
2
6. The Trial Court, by its order dated 25.08.2025 dismissed the
said interlocutory application on the ground that it is too late to
seek an amendment. Against the said order, the respondent filed a
Revision before the High Court, which came to be allowed in the
order impugned before us.
7. Order 6 Rule 17’s proviso reads thus;
Amendment of pleadings.— The Court may at any stage of
the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend
his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may
be just, and all such amendments shall be made as may
be necessary for the purpose of determining the real
questions in controversy between the parties: 
Provided that no application for amendment shall be
allowed after the trial has commenced, unless the
Court comes to the conclusion that in spite of due
diligence, the party could not have raised the matter
before the commencement of trial. 
8. Having  heard  learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  and  the
respondent, we are of the opinion that the Trial Court rightly
dismissed the interlocutory application which has been filed after
more than five years. It is also important to take note of the fact
that the evidence has commenced and as such, allowing such an
amendment is contrary to proviso to Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of
Civil Procedure.
9. In that view of the matter, we set aside the order passed by
the High Court. Since the suit is of the year 2019, we request the
Trial Court to dispose of the suit as expeditiously as possible. We
also make it clear that we have not expressed any opinion on the
merits of the matter and our directions are confined only to the

--- Page 411 ---
3
interlocutory application filed under Order 6 Rule 17 of CPC.
10. In view of the above, the civil appeal is allowed. No order as
to costs.

1. The appellant challenges the judgment and order dated
16.07.2025 in CRRP No.1581/2016 titled “N.T. Kantharaju vs.
S. Nagraj (since deceased by his Lrs.)” passed by the High
Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru.
2. We notice that the Trial Court convicted the appellant
for  the  offence  punishable  under  section  138  of  the
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and awarded compensation of
Rs.3,00,000/-with fine of Rs.10,000/- and in default to
undergo simple imprisonment for a period of six months which
was affirmed by the Appellate Court.  The High Court vide
impugned  order  dated  16.07.2025  allowed  the  Criminal
Revision Petition.
3. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
4. Considering the nature of offence, we are inclined to
modify the impugned  order passed  by  the High Court and to
1

--- Page 425 ---
put a quietus to the matter, direct the appellant to pay a

deposited within a period of four weeks from today. Let the

respondent No.1. The particulars of the bank account of
respondent No.1 shall be immediately supplied by the learned

  M/S ARYAN ENERGY PRIVATE LTD                       APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
THE SINGARENI COLLERIE COMPANY LTD & ANR.          RESPONDENT(S) 
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. The appeal lies on a very short compass. 
3. It is filed against the order passed by the Trial Court, later
confirmed by the High Court, wherein the application filed by
the appellant for production of additional documents, was
rejected on the ground of delay. 
4. It is not in dispute that the suit is one for recovery of
money. The appellant before us is the plaintiff. The document
sought  to  be  produced  are  the  documents  issued  by  the
respondent(s) themselves. In other words, in any case the
documents are not in dispute. 
5. In our considered view, both the Courts have adopted a very
hyper technical approach in rejecting the application, merely
on the ground of delay. Suffice, it is to state that the
appellant being a plaintiff has to prove his case to the
satisfaction of the Trial Court. 
6. In such view of the matter, the impugned order passed by the

--- Page 452 ---
2
High Court confirming the order of the Trial Court stands set
aside. The application for production of additional documents
stands  allowed.  The  respondents  are  permitted  to  file
additional written statement, if any, within a period of six
weeks thereafter. 
7. The appeal is allowed in above terms. 
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.   3445   OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 10023/2026)
SHIMBHU SINGH      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of  Madhya
Pradesh.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 27.04.2026
passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
prayer for anticipatory bail of the appellant.
4. Appellant has been arrayed as an accused in Crime
No.133/2024 registered at Police Station- Maksudangarh,
District- Guna, Madhya Pradesh under Sections 109(1),
31(2), 311, 191(2), 191(3), 190, 118(1), 118(2) of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNS’).
5. This Court by order dated 02.06.2026 had issued
notice and granted interim protection to the appellant on
condition that appellant would deposit his passport, if he
possesses one, before the competent authority/Court and
1

--- Page 491 ---
would also make himself available before the Investigating
Officer on 12.06.2026 at 10:00 AM.
6. In  the  hearing  today,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State of Madhya Pradesh submits that appellant
had  appeared  before  the  Investigating  Officer  on
12.06.2026 and his statement has been recorded.
7. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  submits  that
thereafter he has not been summoned by the Investigating
Officer.
8. In such circumstances, we are inclined to make our
order dated 02.06.2026 absolute.
9. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned order dated
27.04.2026 passed by the High Court and make the order
dated  02.06.2026  absolute.  However,  appellant  shall
continue to co-operate with the investigation of the case.
10. Consequently, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 3470 OF 2026
[ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRL) NO.825/2026]
AVICHAL KUMAR                         Appellant(s)
VERSUS
STATE OF UP & ANR.                   Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
The appellant was charged in Case Crime
No.1053/2017,  dated  24.09.2017  registered  at
Police Station: Chakeri, District: Kanpur Nagar
for the offences punishable under Sections 420,
467, 468, 471, 406, 504 and 506 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860.  
His  application  seeking  discharge  was
dismissed  by  the  Trial  Court,  and  a  criminal
review  filed  against  the  said  order  was  also
dismissed  by  the  High  Court.  Aggrieved,  the
present appeal has been filed.
The short submission made by the learned
counsel for the appellant is that the High Court
has committed an error in dismissing the petition
filed, without going into the merits of the case,
on the sole premise that the appellant has not
placed  the  charge  sheet  and  the  statement  of
prosecution witnesses on record.

--- Page 494 ---
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted
that when the challenge was made, chargesheet was
not filed by the investigating agency. He further
submits that the approach of the High Court is
rather technical, and the appellant ought to have
been given an opportunity to place the same on
record.
Learned counsel for the respondent submitted
that  the  charge  sheet  was  available  with  the
appellant  at  the  relevant  point  of  time  and
therefore, there is no need for any interference.
Considering  the  submissions,  while  not
interfering  with  the  impugned  order,  we  give
liberty to the appellant to challenge the charge
sheet, in which case the impugned order will not
act as a bar.
The  Criminal  Appeal  is  disposed  of,
accordingly.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.
. . . . . . . . .,J

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal  No(s).  3439/2026
SLP (Crl.) No(s). 11310/2026
RAJKUMAR                                           Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ANR.                     Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order dated
20.04.2026 passed by the High Court of Madhya
Pradesh at Indore rejecting the regular bail
prayer of the appellant in connection with
Crime No. 454/2020, registered at P.S. M.P.
Government  through  Forest  Range  Officer,
Dhamnod, District Dhar. 
4. The submission on behalf of the learned
counsel for the appellant is that the offences
concerned  are  all  triable  by  a  Court  of
Magistrate and would result in a term sentence
if convicted; whereas the appellant has been in
jail since 19.09.2025. In such circumstances,
it  has  been  prayed  that  the  appellant  be
1

--- Page 500 ---
released on bail. 
5.  The  learned  Counsel  for  the  State-
respondent has opposed the prayer for bail but
could not demonstrate as to on what basis one
of the charging sections relate to an offence
under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. 
6. Having  regard  to  the  nature  of  the
allegations against the appellant, we are of
the view that the appellant is entitled to be
released on bail at this stage.
7.  Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The
order passed by the High Court rejecting the
regular bail prayer of the appellant is set
aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on bail
on such terms and conditions as the trial court
may  deem  fit  to  impose  in  the  facts  and
circumstances of the case. 
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

1. Mr. Amit Anand Tiwari and Mr. Rahul Kaushik, learned
Senior Counsel, would submit that petitioners are compelled
to  prefer  these  petition(s)  under  Article  32  of  the
Constitution of India, despite the dismissal of their
1

--- Page 521 ---
Original Application on 19.03.2014, Writ Petition by the
Delhi High Court on 14.10.2019, and Special Leave Petition
by this Court on 24.10.2017. 
2. The petitioner(s) submit that the Original Application
of similarly situated candidates, who were recruited in the
same  recruitment  process,  was  allowed  by  the  Central
Administrative Tribunal on 26.07.2024, which was affirmed
by the Delhi High Court on 11.08.2025, against which the
Special Leave Petition preferred by the Union of India (SLP
(Civil) Diary No. 72943/2025) was dismissed on 27.01.2026,
keeping the question of law open.
3. Thus, there are two different sets of orders in respect
of two sets of candidates who were recruited in the same
recruitment process. 
4. Be that as it may, the fact remains that in the
petitioners' Original Application which traveled up to the
SLP, they have failed, and their termination has been held
valid.
5. Thus, a  lis inter-parties  cannot be reopened in
exercise of powers under Article 32 of the Constitution of
India, as this Court will not set aside its own order
passed in an SLP by exercising writ jurisdiction under
Article 32 of Constitution of India.
6. Accordingly, we hold that the Writ Petition(s) are not
maintainable, however, the petitioners may avail any other
remedy as is available to them under the law, including
filing of a Miscellaneous Application (MA) or a Review
2

--- Page 522 ---
Petition, as the case may be.

of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. These petitions arise from the Order passed by the High Court
of Judicature at Madras dated 7-8-2025 in Writ Appeal No.1951/2024
filed by the State of Tamil Nadu and Writ Appeal filed by the
Respondent No.6. Both the appeals came to be allowed.
2. The  subject  –  matter  of  the  present  litigation  is  the
conversion of the industrial land for residential purposes.
3. It is the case of the petitioner – Association that way back
in 1937, the entire area in question started developing as an
industrial area. There are hundreds of industries at the place
called Salem Camp situated on the banks of river Cauvery.
4. According to the petitioner – Association with the conversion
of the use of land, people will now start constructing residential
colonies and that may disturb the entire working of the industries
in the area, more particularly the chemical industries.
5. We  heard  Mr.  Vinay  Navare,  the  learned  Senior  counsel
appearing  for  the  petitioner  –  Association  and  Mr.  V.P.
Sengottuvel,  the  learned  Senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
Respondent No.6.
6. We are of the view that no error not to speak of any error of
law could be said to have been committed by the High Court in
passing the impugned Judgments and Orders.
7. We make it clear that since the Government on its own has
decided to change the use of land and is now going to permit coming
up of residential colonies also, the residents of the area shall
not  raise  any  objection  as  regards  the  functioning  of  the
industries, except if they are not running it in accordance with
law. In other words, we make it clear that if the Respondent No.6
intends to develop this area and utilize it for residential
purpose, it shall make itself public and bring it to the people at
large that it has given an undertaking before the Supreme Court
that they would not raise any objection as regards running of the
industries in the area concerned including the purchasers of the
residential houses/apartments.

--- Page 537 ---
3
8. With the aforesaid, these petitions stand disposed of.
9. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

Court, Secunderabad, Telangana within a period of six

        UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
The writ petition before the High Court, filed
by the wife (petitioner no.1) and daughters (petitioner
nos. 2 and 3) of the deceased, sought two reliefs,
firstly, a fair investigation into the custodial death
of  the  deceased  and  secondly,  compensation  of
Rs.50,00,000/- on account of the custodial death.
1

--- Page 617 ---
The High Court disposed of the writ petition by
awarding  Rs.1,00,000/-  as  compensation  and  without
issuing any direction for the registration of an F.I.R.
and investigation into the matter.
Notice was issued in the present special leave
petition on 08.01.2026.
A counter affidavit has been filed by the State
of Chhattisgarh. However, it does not disclose the
steps taken with respect to lodging of the F.I.R. and
the investigation into the custodial death of the
husband of petitioner no.1 and father of petitioner
nos. 2 and 3.
Further, the amount of compensation awarded by
the High Court appears to be completely inadequate and
not commensurate with the gravity of the loss suffered
by the petitioners.
Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Chhattisgarh shall obtain instructions within a week.
List the matter again on 04.08.2026.
On the said date, the Director General of Police
and  Principal  Secretary  (Home)  for  the  State  of
Chhattisgarh,  to  remain  present  through  video
conference.

Petition(s) for Special Leave to Appeal (Crl.)  No(s).  5379/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated  22-08-2025
in CRLA No. 630/2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Madras]
JEYACHANDRAN                                       Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA                                     Respondent(s)
IA No. 78083/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
 
Date : 27-07-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE ARAVIND KUMAR
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIPUL M. PANCHOLI
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. G. Murugendran, Adv.
                   Mr. Navneet Dugar, AOR
                   
                   
For Respondent(s) :Mr. Vikramjit Banerjee, A.S.G.
                   Mr. Akshat Agarwal, Adv.
                   Ms. Aastha Singh, Adv.
                   Mr. Ishaan Sharma, Adv.
                   Mr. Mukesh Kumar Singh, Adv.
                   Mr. Yogesh Vats, Adv.
                   Dr. N. Visakamurthy, AOR
                                      
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard learned counsel appearing for the petitioner and Shri
Vikramjit Banerjee, learned ASG, appearing for the respondent-Union
of India.
2. The prosecution case is that, acting on prior intelligence, NCB
intercepted  A1  to  A3  (including  the  petitioner  herein)  on
1

--- Page 789 ---
07.01.2019 and based on their disclosure statements, recovered
107.02 kgs of ganja from A4 and A5 on the next day. Petitioner, who
is arraigned as A2, is alleged to be a part of the conspiracy and
all the accused had prior knowledge of the contraband and they
facilitated transportation of the contraband. It is contended that
disclosure statement of petitioner led to the recovery of the
contraband  from  A4  and  A5,  thereby  indicating  his  conscious
possession and participation in the offence.
3. Learned Sessions Court, after trial, convicted all five accused
persons for offence punishable under Sections 20(b)(ii)(c), 28 and
29 of Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (NDPS
Act) and sentenced them to 10 years rigorous imprisonment.
4. The petitioner herein has undisputedly undergone imprisonment
for more than 4 years 10 months and 27 days. The alleged recovery
from A4 and A5 is said to be on the basis of the confessional
statement of the petitioner herein.  Prima facie  reading of the
statement would indicate that the statement is recorded in a
prototype manner.
5. Be that as it may, at this stage, we are of the considered view
that petitioner is not having any criminal antecedents and recovery
having not been made from his conscious possession, the grounds
urged in the present petition cannot be brushed aside. As such, we
suspend the sentence imposed by the learned trial Judge as affirmed
by the High Court and order for release of the petitioner on bail
by the jurisdictional court on such terms and conditions as it
deems fit.
6. List this matter for hearing in the second week of January,
2027. In the meanwhile call for the lower court records.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
We have heard learned Senior Counsel appearing for
the petitioner, and learned counsel appearing for the
respondent-State.
It is not that we are dealing with a case of a
license that was renewed after coming into force of the
Targeted Public Distribution System (Control) Order, 2015
(‘2015 Central Order’). Cancellation of the license was
passed under the Gujarat Essential Commodities (Licensing
to Fair Price Shop) Order, 2004 (‘2004 State Order’).
1

--- Page 965 ---
Though the learned counsel for the petitioner seeks
to rely upon Clause 9 to be read along with Clause 1(2) of
the ‘2015 Central Order’, even then the petitioner will
have no right for the simple reason that the State Order
has come into force in terms of Clause 9. Therefore, even
if we read the provision, which is the correct approach,
the petitioner will not have any right.
The  Special  Leave  Petition  is,  accordingly,
dismissed.
However, this order passed will not stand in the way
of the petitioner invoking the appellate remedy.
Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

For Respondent(s): 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard learned counsel for the petitioner.
2. The High Court declined to entertain the Criminal  
Appeal of the petitioner assailing his conviction under 
Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short,  
‘IPC’) on the ground of inordinate delay. Petitioner is 
in custody for more than 12 years now. For delay of  
2538 days in filing the Criminal Appeal, the High Court 
1

--- Page 1019 ---
dismissed the same.
3. Prima facie, we are of the view that when the  
convict is in jail and this being a jail appeal, the  
same ought not to have been dismissed on the ground of  
delay and should have been heard on merits. In such  
circumstances ordinarily we would have remanded the  
matter  to  the  High  Court  for  hearing  on  merits. 
However, having regard to the fact that petitioner has  
already undergone incarceration of more than 12 years,  
we do not propose to remand the matter back to the High 
Court.
4. The delay in filing the Special Leave Petition is  
condoned.
5. Issue notice, both on the Special Leave Petition  
as well as on the prayer for bail, returnable on  
03.09.2026.
6. Permission is accorded to learned counsel for the  
petitioner to serve notice upon the Standing counsel  
for the respondent-State of Odisha.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Having regard to the bar of Section 37 of the
Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
1

--- Page 1059 ---
as also that trial has commenced and 4 out of 20
witnesses have already been examined, we do not find
it to be a fit case for consideration of bail prayer
at this stage.
2. The  Special  Leave  Petition  is,  accordingly,
disposed of by issuing a direction upon the trial
court to ensure completion of trial expeditiously
preferably within a period of six months from the
date of  a  certified copy of this order is placed
before the Trial Court.
3. In case the trial is not completed within the
aforesaid  period,  it  shall  be  open  for  the

Punjab and Haryana, the concerned Committee of the High
1

--- Page 1083 ---
Court  passed  a  resolution  in  the  meeting  held  on
08.11.2012, recommending to the Government of Punjab to
rectify the anomaly by granting to the Restorers a pay band
of 10,300 – 34,800 with a grade pay of 3,200, as₹ ₹ ₹
admissible to Clerks.
3. However, when this recommendation was not acted
upon, the concerned Restorers preferred a writ petition
before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in CWP No. 488
of 2015 (O&M), which was allowed by the High Court on
16.01.2015, and has since been acted upon by the State of
Punjab.

Restorer working in the State Legal Services Authority,
Chandigarh, however, the judgment rendered by the High
Court would not apply to the petitioner on the ground that
the  State  Legal  Services  Authority  is  a  different
establishment,  and  consequently,  the  petitioner's  writ
petition has been dismissed, despite a similar order being
passed in favor of Restorers working in the High Court.

1. The  petitioner  who  has  been  in  judicial  custody  since
04.08.2023  for  2  years  &  9  months  in  connection  with  FIR
No. 298/2023 dated 13.06.2023, filed at PS Patel Nagar, District
Dehradun, Uttarakhand under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 is seeking regular bail.

--- Page 1203 ---
2
2. The petitioner is accused of assaulting the injured deceased
with a rod causing grievous injuries leading to his death. The
Trial Court and High Court rejected the petitioner’s plea for
regular bail on the grounds of non-examination of witnesses &
considering the serious nature of crime. 
3. The learned Counsel for the petitioner submitted that the
investigation is complete & the charge-sheet has been filed. It is
further submitted that, there is no direct or circumstantial
evidence linking the accused to the crime as he was not present at
the spot, which is prima facie supported by the deposition of sole
eye witness (PW6) who has turned hostile during cross examination;
& that there is absence of any incriminating recovery from him. It
is also submitted that out of 18 witnesses, only 10 witnesses have
been examined by the trial court.
4. On a prima facie consideration of the material on record and
after hearing the learned counsel for the parties, we are of the
opinion that the petitioner can be released on bail, subject to
cooperating in the trial and such other terms and conditions that
the Ld.  Sessions Judge, Dehradun  (the jurisdictional court) may
deem fit and appropriate to impose. It is ordered accordingly.
5. With the above directions, the Special Leave Petition is
disposed of.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
 (VISHAL ANAND)                                    (POOJA SHARMA)

    M/S. Nuli & Nuli, AOR 
                   Mr. Abhishek Kanyalur, Adv.

For Respondent(s): 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard Mr. Anand Sanjay M. Nuli, learned  
Senior counsel for the petitioner.
2. Delay condoned.
3. Learned Senior counsel for the petitioner submits  
that  the  finding  recorded  by  the  High  Court  in  
Paragraph No.09 of the impugned order that once the  
defendant claims that he is the owner of the suit land, 
he cannot claim that he has perfected his title by way  
1

--- Page 1241 ---
of adverse possession, is contrary to a judgment of  
this Court rendered in  L.N. Aswathama and Another  
versus  P.  Prakash  [(2009)  13  SCC  229]  where  in  
Paragraph No.18, this Court has held that the plea of  
title and the plea of adverse possession are not  
inconsistent pleas but alternative pleas available on  
the same facts.
4. Issue notice, returnable on 05.10.2026.
5. In the meanwhile, parties shall maintain status  
quo as regards the suit property.

For Respondent(s) : 
           UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Since  the  matter  pertains  to  appointment  of  public
appointments in the State of Andhra Praesh, we decline to entertain
this  Writ  Petition  at  this  stage  and  grant  liberty  to  the
petitioner to approach the jurisdictional High Court.
2. The Writ Petition is, accordingly, dismissed.
3. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand closed.
